components.name: build-agent
components.why_use: Reach for build-agent when an orchestrator needs to fan out file creation across a parallel build — each instance owns exactly one file, gathers its own context, implements, and self-verifies, so the full build completes in one coordinated wave instead of serially. It directly embodies TAC Lesson 13's meta-agentics principle: agents building agents, where the orchestrating layer issues atomic work units that can run concurrently without cross-agent coordination.

frontmatter.name: build-agent
frontmatter.description: Use proactively when you need to delegate writing a single file as part of a parallel build workflow. Specialist for implementing one specific file based on detailed instructions and context.
frontmatter.tools: Write, Read, Edit, Grep, Glob, Bash, TodoWrite

components.name: docs-scraper
components.why_use: Reach for docs-scraper when you need to hydrate an agent's offline reference library before a self-improve or plan run — it automates the LEARN phase by pulling live documentation into ai_docs/ so downstream experts can read it without hitting the network. It is especially valuable in Act-Learn-Reuse pipelines where fresh vendor docs need to be captured once and reused across many agent invocations rather than re-fetched on every execution.

frontmatter.name: docs-scraper
frontmatter.description: Documentation scraping specialist. Use proactively to fetch and save documentation from URLs as properly formatted markdown files.

components.name: meta-agent
components.why_use: Reach for this component when you need to spin up a new Claude Code sub-agent without hand-writing the configuration file — it enforces structural correctness (frontmatter, four required sections, tool minimalism) so the resulting agent is immediately usable. In TAC terms, this is the meta-agentics layer: the system that builds the system, letting you expand your agentic bench faster than manual scaffolding allows.

frontmatter.name: meta-agent
frontmatter.description: Generates a new, complete Claude Code sub-agent configuration file from a user's description. Use this to create new agents. Use this Proactively when the user asks you to create a new sub agent.

components.name: planner
components.why_use: Reach for this agent when you want every planning request to flow through the canonical /plan command rather than being resolved ad-hoc by whatever agent is in context. As the lesson frames it, this is a meta-agentic building block — a thin wrapper that standardizes delegation so the underlying plan skill can evolve independently of all callers.

frontmatter.name: planner
frontmatter.description: Delegate to this agent when the user wants to create a structured plan, break down a task into steps, or needs strategic planning for a feature or project

components.name: playwright-validator
components.why_use: Reach for playwright-validator when you need deterministic proof that a UI flow works — not just that the code ships clean, but that a real browser executed the path and screenshots confirm it. It's the Act step made concrete: it takes a useful browser action, captures visual evidence at every transition, and emits a structured report that downstream agents or humans can reason about.

frontmatter.name: playwright-validator
frontmatter.description: Specialized browser automation validator that uses Playwright MCP tools to execute and validate specific user actions on web pages. Use proactively to test web interactions, capture screenshots, and verify UI behaviors with comprehensive reporting.
frontmatter.tools: mcp__playwright__browser_navigate, mcp__playwright__browser_snapshot, mcp__playwright__browser_take_screenshot, mcp__playwright__browser_click, mcp__playwright__browser_type, mcp__playwright__browser_fill_form, mcp__playwright__browser_wait_for, mcp__playwright__browser_evaluate, mcp__playwright__browser_select, mcp__playwright__browser_hover, mcp__playwright__browser_press, mcp__playwright__browser_scroll, mcp__playwright__browser_get_cookies, mcp__playwright__browser_set_cookies, mcp__playwright__browser_clear_cookies, mcp__playwright__browser_reload, mcp__playwright__browser_back, mcp__playwright__browser_forward, mcp__playwright__browser_set_viewport, Write, Edit

components.name: scout-report-suggest-fast
components.why_use: Reach for this agent when you need a precise damage report before touching any code — it scouts file locations, root causes, and cascading dependencies without mutating state, so downstream acting agents receive a high-signal brief instead of guessing. In TAC terms, it is the dedicated ACT-phase scout that feeds the LEARN and REUSE steps with grounded evidence rather than hallucinated assumptions.

frontmatter.name: scout-report-suggest-fast
frontmatter.description: Use proactively to scout codebase issues, identify problem locations, and suggest resolutions. Specialist for read-only analysis and reporting without making changes.

components.name: scout-report-suggest
components.why_use: Reach for scout-report-suggest when you need a safe, read-only investigation pass before any code modification — it separates the 'understand the problem' phase from the 'fix the problem' phase, reducing the risk of premature or wrong-target edits. In the Act-Learn-Reuse pattern it anchors the Act step by surfacing exact file paths, line numbers, and root causes that downstream agents or humans can act on with confidence.

frontmatter.name: scout-report-suggest
frontmatter.description: Use proactively to scout codebase issues, identify problem locations, and suggest resolutions. Specialist for read-only analysis and reporting without making changes.

components.name: all_tools
components.why_use: Reach for this command when you need to inspect the full capability surface of an agent before designing or debugging—knowing exactly which tools are wired up prevents planning around primitives that don't exist in the current context. In the Act-Learn-Reuse pattern it serves as a fast bootstrap step: before an agent expert can Act effectively, the engineer must confirm which tools are actually on the table.

components.name: build_in_parallel
components.why_use: Reach for this command when a multi-file implementation plan exists and sequential file-by-file coding would be the bottleneck — it fans out one build-agent per file so all independent files land simultaneously. It embodies the Act-Learn-Reuse pattern at the build layer: gather full context once, delegate richly specified tasks in parallel, and collapse the results into a cohesive delivery.

frontmatter.description: Build the codebase in parallel by delegating file creation to build-agents

components.name: build
components.why_use: Reach for /build when you have a written plan file and want an agent to drive the full implementation to completion without human checkpoints — it enforces top-to-bottom sequential execution and mandates self-validation before stopping. In Act-Learn-Reuse terms this is the 'Act' phase made agentic: the plan is the input, a validated codebase change is the output.

frontmatter.description: Build the codebase based on the plan

components.name: question
components.why_use: Reach for this command when you need authoritative, validated answers about the database layer without touching a single file — it is the pure Reuse step of the Act-Learn-Reuse pattern, drawing on the agent's accumulated expertise.yaml before confirming against live code. Use it to short-circuit the impulse to manually grep through schema files or Pydantic models whenever a teammate or PR review surface a data-architecture question.

frontmatter.description: Answer questions about database schema, models, and operations without coding

components.name: self-improve
components.why_use: Reach for this command after database schema changes, new migrations, or significant query refactoring to keep the Database expert's mental model synchronized with reality. It embodies the LEARN step of the Act-Learn-Reuse pattern—letting the agent self-correct its expertise file so every future expert invocation reuses accurate, codebase-verified knowledge rather than stale assumptions.

components.name: plan_build_improve
components.why_use: Reach for this command when you want a single invocation to carry a WebSocket feature from blank slate to working code *and* leave the agent smarter for the next run — it chains plan → build → self-improve without requiring you to babysit each step. It is the canonical instantiation of the Act-Learn-Reuse pattern from Lesson 13: the agent acts (builds), learns (self-improves expertise), and the updated expertise file is ready to reuse on the next execution.

components.name: plan
components.why_use: Reach for this component when a planning task touches WebSocket architecture and you want accumulated domain knowledge—not just file reads—baked into the plan before /plan ever runs. It is the REUSE leg of the Act-Learn-Reuse pattern: expertise already earned by self-improve passes is injected as a mental model so the planner never starts from zero on WebSocket-specific patterns, edge cases, or critical files.

frontmatter.allowed-tools: Read, SlashCommand, TodoWrite, Grep, Glob, Bash
frontmatter.description: Create WebSocket-focused implementation plan using expertise context

components.name: question
components.why_use: Reach for this when you need authoritative, codebase-validated answers about WebSocket architecture without risking accidental code changes — it is the Reuse leg of the Act-Learn-Reuse pattern, letting accumulated expertise in the expertise.yaml pay off on demand. Use it when onboarding to a complex real-time system or sanity-checking architectural assumptions before planning a change.

frontmatter.description: Answer questions about websocket management in this codebase without coding

components.name: self-improve
components.why_use: Reach for this command whenever WebSocket-related code changes and the expert's mental model risks drifting from reality — it walks the codebase, diffs the expertise YAML against actual implementation, and self-heals discrepancies so the next expert invocation reasons from current knowledge rather than stale assumptions. It is the concrete 'Learn' step of the Act-Learn-Reuse pattern from Lesson 13: running it until stable is what separates a domain expert that compounds knowledge from a generic agent that forgets between sessions.

components.name: find_and_summarize
components.why_use: Reach for this command when you need a systematic, structured inventory of files across a directory — it reads each file incrementally and emits a two-sentence YAML summary per file, ready to feed into expertise files or onboarding docs. In the Act-Learn-Reuse cycle, it powers the Learn step by converting raw codebase content into reusable reference artifacts that future agents can consume without re-reading source files.

frontmatter.description: Finds and summarizes specific files in the codebase and saves the summary to app_docs directory

components.name: load_ai_docs
components.why_use: Reach for this component when your agents need fresh external documentation as context without incurring a network fetch on every run — it implements a TTL-gated cache so docs stay current without redundant scraping. Ground in Lesson 13: this is meta-agentic infrastructure that 'builds the system that builds', provisioning the knowledge layer agents consume before they Act-Learn-Reuse.

frontmatter.description: Load documentation from their respective websites into local markdown files our agents can use as context.
frontmatter.allowed-tools: Task, WebFetch, Write, Edit, Bash(ls*), mcp__firecrawl-mcp__firecrawl_scrape

components.name: load_bundle
components.why_use: Reach for this command when a multi-agent pipeline needs one agent to pick up exactly where a predecessor left off — it reconstructs the predecessor's file-read context from a JSONL bundle so the successor wastes no tokens re-discovering already-loaded state. In TAC's Act-Learn-Reuse terms, it converts a previous agent's Act phase into the Reuse starting point for the next agent, making context continuity automatic across handoffs.

frontmatter.description: Understand the previous agents context and load files from a context bundle with their original read parameters

components.name: meta_prompt
components.why_use: Reach for meta_prompt when you need to scaffold a new slash command without writing it by hand — it operationalizes the Meta Agentics principle from TAC Lesson 13 ('prompts writing prompts, agents building agents') so your agentic layer grows faster with each new domain. Use it whenever a repeated workflow or emerging expert domain needs a purpose-built command and you want the AI to handle spec compliance, documentation fetching, and file output itself.

frontmatter.allowed-tools: Write, Edit, WebFetch, Task, mcp__firecrawl-mcp__firecrawl_scrape, Fetch
frontmatter.description: Create a new prompt based on a user's request

components.name: parallel_subagents
components.why_use: Reach for this command when a task decomposes into N independent subtasks that benefit from simultaneous execution—instead of chaining agents serially, you fan-out in one batch and synthesize results, collapsing wall-clock time. It embodies TAC's meta-agentics principle: rather than writing code yourself, you're building the coordination layer that spawns and directs agents on your behalf.

components.name: plan_w_scouters
components.why_use: Reach for this command when planning a non-trivial feature, refactor, or fix in a large or unfamiliar codebase — it deploys 8 parallel scout subagents (3 base + 5 fast) to divide-and-conquer codebase exploration before any design is committed, then consolidates findings into a validated spec. It operationalizes the TAC principle of prioritizing agentics over manual linear reads: instead of one agent sequentially grepping, a swarm fans out simultaneously and the human only reviews the finished plan artifact.

frontmatter.description: Creates a concise engineering implementation plan based on user requirements and saves it to specs directory

components.name: plan
components.why_use: Reach for this command when you need to convert loose requirements into a structured, reviewable implementation blueprint before writing any code — it makes Tactic 1 (stop coding, plan first) executable by externalizing architecture decisions, edge cases, and ordered tasks into a durable spec file. In the Act-Learn-Reuse paradigm from Lesson 13, the produced spec is the reusable artifact that downstream agents and developers execute against without rethinking from scratch.

frontmatter.description: Creates a concise engineering implementation plan based on user requirements and saves it to specs directory

components.name: prime_cc
components.why_use: Reach for prime_cc when an agent needs to orient itself specifically within the Claude Code configuration layer before proposing or executing improvements—it front-loads situational awareness of commands, hooks, skills, and agents so subsequent work is grounded in actual repo structure. In TAC terms, this is the 'Reuse' half of Act-Learn-Reuse: the agent reads accumulated expertise (the .claude/ tree) before acting, preventing repeated discovery work across sessions.

frontmatter.description: Gain a general understanding of the codebase with a focus on Claude Code improvements

components.name: prime_nile
components.why_use: Reach for prime_nile when any agent is about to work on the Nile application cold — it bulk-loads every critical file via @ references so the agent arrives context-rich and can immediately reason about the ACT → LEARN → REUSE cycle without spending tokens on exploration. In TAC terms this is the mandatory warm-start step before invoking any Nile-specific expert, planner, or build command, embodying the meta-agentics principle that the system which builds must itself be built deliberately.

frontmatter.allowed-tools: Read, Glob, Grep, Bash, Edit, Write, Task
frontmatter.description: Prime agents with comprehensive understanding of the Nile adaptive shopping application

components.name: prime
components.why_use: Reach for `prime.md` at the start of any session where the agent needs a grounded mental model of the orchestrator codebase before acting — it front-loads context so subsequent commands (plan, build, self-improve) operate with accurate codebase awareness rather than hallucinated assumptions. In the Act-Learn-Reuse pattern from Lesson 13, this is the mandatory pre-Act step: without it, even well-designed experts work on stale or incomplete context.

components.name: question-w-mermaid-diagrams
components.why_use: Reach for this command when you need to understand or communicate project structure, data flows, or component relationships and a textual answer alone would leave the mental model incomplete. It is the right tool when onboarding, auditing architecture, or explaining a system to stakeholders who benefit from visual artifacts over prose.

frontmatter.description: Answer questions about the project structure and documentation with Mermaid diagrams

components.name: question
components.why_use: Reach for this command when you need to interrogate a project's structure or documentation without risking any file mutations — it enforces a hard read-only contract at the prompt level. In TAC terms it is the safe 'Act' precursor: gather context and understanding before you build, plan, or self-improve.

frontmatter.description: Answer questions about the project structure and documentation without coding

components.name: quick-plan
components.why_use: Reach for this when you need to convert a vague requirement into a structured implementation blueprint before any coding begins — it front-loads deep reasoning so the build phase becomes pure execution with no ambiguity. In TAC terms it embodies the dedicated planner role in a multi-agent pipeline: one agent plans, another builds, keeping concerns cleanly separated rather than collapsed into a single context.

components.name: start_nile
components.why_use: Reach for this command when you need to spin up the full Nile dev stack — FastAPI backend and Vue frontend — with a single invocation instead of juggling multiple terminals manually. In TAC terms it eliminates repetitive environment-setup friction so the engineer stays in flow and can immediately move to feature work rather than process management.

frontmatter.description: Start Nile backend (port 8000) and frontend (port 5173) in background processes

components.name: notification.py
components.why_use: Reach for this hook when your agents run in low-attention or background mode and you need a sensory signal—not a screen glance—to know when the agent has stalled waiting for input. It is the physical-world bridge of the Act-Learn-Reuse pattern: the agent Acts until it can't, then this fires to pull the human back in without requiring them to poll a terminal.

components.name: post_tool_use.py
components.why_use: Reach for this hook when you need silent, zero-configuration observability into every tool call an agent makes — it is the foundational 'Learn' infrastructure in the Act-Learn-Reuse cycle, capturing raw event data that self-improve prompts and expertise files can later consume. It is the right primitive when you want persistent telemetry that accumulates autonomously across sessions without any human in the loop.

components.name: pre_compact.py
components.why_use: Reach for this hook when you need to preserve the full conversational transcript before Claude compacts it away — it is the observability layer that makes the Act-Learn-Reuse cycle auditable by ensuring no accumulated context is silently discarded. It is especially critical in Agent Expert workflows where the transcript contains the raw material that the self-improve prompt later mines to update expertise files.

components.name: pre_tool_use.py
components.why_use: Reach for this hook when deploying agents at high autonomy levels where destructive or sensitive operations must be blocked before execution — it intercepts every tool call automatically, providing a non-negotiable safety floor. In TAC terms, this is the infrastructure that makes zero-touch Act-Learn-Reuse loops viable; without pre-tool-use guards, autonomous agents operating on real filesystems have no protection against catastrophic side effects.

components.name: send_event.py
components.why_use: Reach for this hook when you need real-time telemetry on what your Claude Code agents are actually doing across sessions — it is the observability backbone that makes the Act→Learn→Reuse cycle auditable. In multi-agent systems (Lesson 13), forgetfulness is the enemy; this script captures the 'Act' layer so downstream expertise files and summaries have raw signal to learn from.

components.name: session_start.py
components.why_use: Reach for this component when you need automatic, no-intervention context collection at the start of every agent session — git state, open issues, and session metadata get logged before the agent takes its first action. In the Act-Learn-Reuse pattern from Lesson 13, this hook is the passive infrastructure that feeds the Learn phase: it captures environmental snapshots so downstream experts and self-improve prompts have grounded, timestamped context to reason over.

components.name: stop.py
components.why_use: Reach for this hook when you want the Act→Learn→Reuse loop to close without the engineer watching the terminal — it fires on every Claude stop event and delivers an auditory or LLM-generated completion signal so the developer can stay heads-down on other work. It embodies Tactic 1 (stop coding, let agents run) by making zero-touch agent sessions feel supervised without actually requiring supervision.

components.name: subagent_stop.py
components.why_use: Reach for this hook when running multi-agent Act-Learn-Reuse pipelines where subagents operate autonomously and you need ambient awareness of completion without polling or watching a terminal — it closes the human feedback loop at the boundary between the Act and Learn phases. It embodies zero-touch observability: the engineer hears a spoken signal and knows the next pipeline stage can proceed, reducing cognitive overhead during long autonomous runs.

components.name: user_prompt_submit.py
components.why_use: Reach for this hook when you need zero-touch observability into every user prompt before any agent action fires — it is the capture layer that makes the Learn step of Act-Learn-Reuse possible by persisting raw session data autonomously. In the Agent Experts pattern, you cannot build a self-improving expertise file without first recording what actually happened; this hook is the always-on recorder that feeds that pipeline.

components.name: constants.py
components.why_use: Reach for this module whenever a hook script needs reproducible, session-scoped log paths — it centralises the ENV-override logic so every hook in the system writes to the same directory tree without duplicating resolution code. In the Act-Learn-Reuse pattern this is the silent foundation of the LEARN step: hooks that record tool events or session artifacts all converge on the same path contract defined here.

components.name: anth.py
components.why_use: Reach for this when a hook needs a sub-100ms LLM call without spinning up a full agent — it wraps Haiku (fastest Anthropic model) with silent failure semantics so the hook never blocks or crashes Claude. In the Act-Learn-Reuse pattern from Lesson 13, this is the Act leaf: it lets any hook emit LLM-generated natural language without boilerplate beyond a single env var.

components.name: oai.py
components.why_use: Reach for this component when a hook needs a lightweight, fire-and-forget LLM call without pulling in the full Claude SDK — it abstracts the fastest OpenAI model behind a single function so hook scripts stay thin. In the Act-Learn-Reuse pattern it sits at the seam between Act and Learn, providing the inference layer that lets hooks generate human-readable signals (e.g. completion messages) autonomously at session end.

components.name: ollama.py
components.why_use: Reach for this when a hook needs lightweight, local LLM inference without cloud API keys or round-trip latency — it wraps Ollama's OpenAI-compatible endpoint so any hook can call a model with one function. It is the infrastructure muscle behind the Act phase of the Act-Learn-Reuse pattern: hooks fire on Claude events, and this utility gives them the model call needed to generate meaningful, personalized output each cycle.

components.name: model_extractor.py
components.why_use: Reach for this component when a hook needs to know which Claude model is active without paying the cost of re-parsing the full JSONL transcript on every invocation — the TTL cache means only the first hook execution within a session window does real I/O work. It encodes the Act-Learn-Reuse insight at the infrastructure layer: act once to extract model identity, cache that fact, and reuse it across all subsequent hook firings in the same session.

components.name: summarizer.py
components.why_use: Reach for this when you need LLM-powered natural language summaries of Claude Desktop hook events, turning raw JSON payloads into human-readable records. It fits the LEARN phase of the Act-Learn-Reuse pattern—capturing what the agent did in a form that can be stored in expertise files or reviewed to improve the self-improve prompt over time.

components.name: elevenlabs_tts.py
components.why_use: Reach for this component when you want hooks to emit real-time audio feedback during Claude lifecycle events (e.g., stop, error) without any human hand-off — the ~75ms ElevenLabs Flash v2.5 latency keeps it non-blocking even in tight agentic loops. In TAC terms it closes the sensory gap in zero-touch pipelines: an agent can Act and immediately surface that action as audio, making long autonomous runs observable without watching a terminal.

components.name: openai_tts.py
components.why_use: Reach for this hook utility when you want zero-touch ambient feedback during long autonomous loops—it turns agentic output or stop events into spoken audio so the engineer stays aware without watching the terminal. In TAC's Act-Learn-Reuse pattern it pairs cleanly with PostToolUse or Stop hooks, converting agent completions into an audio signal that closes the perception loop without pulling the human back in-loop.

components.name: pyttsx3_tts.py
components.why_use: Reach for this component when you need a zero-dependency, offline audio signal that fires automatically at the end of a hook event — it closes the sensory feedback loop so an engineer knows the agent has finished without watching the terminal. In the Act-Learn-Reuse pattern, reliable human-perceptible completion signals prevent premature interruptions that break autonomous execution chains.

components.name: Bullet Points
components.why_use: Reach for this output-style primitive when your Agent Expert's responses — plans, self-improve diffs, mental model dumps — need to be human-scannable the moment they land; dense prose kills the Act-Learn-Reuse loop because stored expertise that's hard to parse on reuse is expertise that doesn't compound. It's the formatting contract that makes an expert's accumulated knowledge actually legible to both humans and downstream agents re-reading the expertise file.

frontmatter.name: Bullet Points
frontmatter.description: Hierarchical bullet points for quick scanning

components.name: GenUI
components.why_use: Reach for GenUI when an agent's response benefits from visual rendering rather than raw text — data summaries, reports, or code explanations land harder as styled HTML pages than markdown walls. In the Act-Learn-Reuse cycle, it turns each ACT into a tangible, shareable artifact that humans can inspect and validate without reading raw output.

frontmatter.name: GenUI

components.name: HTML Structured
components.why_use: Reach for this style when your agent's output must be rendered directly in a browser or consumed by a downstream HTML parser — it enforces a deterministic, semantically-rich surface that UI renderers and extraction tools can depend on without brittle regex hacks. In TAC's Act-Learn-Reuse loop, a stable structured output contract makes the LEARN step (storing and replaying agent results) far cheaper to implement.

frontmatter.name: HTML Structured

components.name: Markdown Focused

Because Agent Experts Act → Learn → Reuse, pairing them with a markdown-focused style ensures every reused expertise chunk is rendered in its most navigable form across both terminal and web surfaces.

frontmatter.name: Markdown Focused

components.name: observable-tools-diffs-tts
components.why_use: Reach for this output style when you need full situational awareness of an agentic session without manually auditing transcripts—every tool call, every file change, and an audio completion announcement surface automatically at the end of each response. In Act-Learn-Reuse terms it makes the Act phase observable and audible, so an engineer can stay informed across long autonomous runs without being blocked waiting for them.

components.name: observable-tools-diffs
components.why_use: Reach for this output style when you need full audit trails of agentic sessions—every tool invoked and every line changed—so humans can verify or replay what the agent did without re-running it. It directly supports the Act-Learn-Reuse pattern by making the 'Act' phase inspectable, which is a prerequisite for meaningful 'Learn' cycles.

components.name: Table Based
components.why_use: Reach for this output style when your agent must surface structured information to a human reviewer — comparisons, analysis findings, configuration options — where wall-of-prose responses would slow scanning and mask signal. In the Act-Learn-Reuse loop, well-structured table outputs make the LEARN step more reliable: a human or downstream agent can parse expertise updates at a glance rather than extracting them from unstructured prose.

frontmatter.name: Table Based

components.name: TTS Summary

It is the right primitive when human-in-the-loop feedback needs to be ambient and personalized rather than read off a screen.

components.name: TTS Summary
components.why_use: Reach for this component when you want every Claude Code session to auto-report its footprint — git diffs, ordered tool calls, and an audio announcement — without wiring up separate observability tooling. In TAC terms it is a self-improving template meta prompt that wraps the agent's communication layer so the Act step is always audible and traceable.

components.name: Ultra Concise

Pair it with high-autonomy expert agents that already hold accumulated domain knowledge; verbose output only adds noise when the engineer can read code faster than prose.

components.name: YAML Structured

In an Act-Learn-Reuse chain, machine-readable agent output reduces friction when shuttling learned artifacts (file lists, commands, status) into the next executor or expertise file.

components.name: settings.json
components.why_use: Reach for this component when you need full-spectrum lifecycle observability across every Claude agent session — it wires a domain handler plus a telemetry emitter on every hook event so the Act-Learn-Reuse loop has raw signal to learn from without any manual instrumentation. It is the configuration backbone that makes expertise accumulation possible: without it, the agent acts but never feeds the learning pipeline.

components.name: creating-new-skills

In TAC Lesson 13 terms it is the 'Meta Agentics' principle made concrete: instead of hand-authoring each skill, you let the system build the system (skills building skills).

It collapses multi-step environment startup (two servers, port config, session resumption, browser launch) into a single invocation so engineers stay focused on agentic work rather than infrastructure babysitting.

components.name: README

Engineers extending the expert system should update this file whenever a new upstream doc source is needed rather than embedding URLs ad-hoc in individual prompts.

components.name: README

It is a dual-mode output contract: the text response is optimized for speed-scanning while the audio layer handles ambient awareness, making it well-suited for heads-down coding sessions where screen attention is scarce.

frontmatter.name: TTS Summary

components.name: Ultra Concise
components.why_use: Reach for this output style when running high-frequency agentic build loops where every token of narration compounds context waste and slows iteration — it suppresses pleasantries, confirmations, and filler so the model's next token is always a tool call or a result. It is also the right choice when pairing with autonomy/out-loop workflows where the engineer has stepped away and wants raw execution output, not a conversation partner.

frontmatter.name: Ultra Concise
frontmatter.description: Minimal words maximum speed direct actions

components.name: Bullet Points

It enforces a strict formatting contract (dash vs. numbered, max nesting depth, ACTION: prefixes) that downstream agents or human reviewers can rely on consistently.

frontmatter.name: Bullet Points

components.name: YAML Structured

It enforces a fixed YAML envelope (task/details/files/commands/status/next_steps/notes) so any consumer can reliably extract structured metadata without natural-language parsing.

It is the canonical 'does the seatbelt buckle?' probe: if any destructive command in its workflow executes unblocked, your install is incomplete and you should not trust agents with real work yet.

components.name: Damage Control
components.why_use: Reach for this skill when you need structural trust rather than model faith — when you want agents to physically be unable to run destructive commands rather than merely prompted not to. It is the canonical ACT-LEARN-REUSE artifact from this lesson: near-production disaster encoded once into a reusable package, deployable to any codebase via a single install prompt.

frontmatter.name: Damage Control
frontmatter.description: Install, configure, and manage the Claude Code Damage Control security hooks system. Use when user mentions damage control, security hooks, protected paths, blocked commands, install security, or modify protection settings.

components.name: README
components.why_use: Reach for this before running any test-prompt suite against the damage control system — it is the human-readable safety gate that enforces the prerequisite that protection must be installed before you simulate destructive commands. In the ACT-LEARN-REUSE frame it is the 'check your harness before jumping' step: skipping it on a machine without hooks installed turns a drill into a live incident.

components.name: README
components.why_use: Reach for this file when you need the authoritative spec behind the two Claude Code subsystems the damage-control skill wraps — PreToolUse hook event payloads and permission-setting schemas — so you can extend patterns.yaml or debug hook behavior against the source of truth rather than guessing. It is the canonical pointer an engineer should check before adding a new blocked pattern or path-protection rule to ensure the hook contract hasn't changed upstream.

components.name: README
components.why_use: Reach for this README when onboarding an engineer or agent to the damage-control system: it surfaces the full hook-routing diagram, exit-code semantics, and path-protection table in one place so the reader can mentally model what fires before a single command executes. It is also the canonical reference when auditing or extending patterns.yaml — the three-level protection table makes the blast radius of each path type immediately legible without reading source code.

components.name: hello-world-agent
components.why_use: Reach for this agent when you need the simplest possible end-to-end proof that your Claude Code agent wiring, hooks, and WebSearch tool access are all live — it is the minimal viable agent integration test. It also serves as the canonical template showing how a sub-agent should format its reply back to the primary agent using the structured markdown response block.

frontmatter.name: hello-world-agent
frontmatter.description: Simple greeting agent, use proactively when greeting the user. If they say 'hi claude' or 'hi cc' or 'hi claude code' use this agent.

components.name: llm-ai-agents-and-eng-research
components.why_use: Reach for this agent when the LEARN step in ACT-LEARN-REUSE requires external signal — new model releases, framework shifts, or benchmark changes that aren't in the repo. It replaces manual tab-sprawl with a structured, date-gated report you can feed directly into prompt and tool decisions.

frontmatter.name: llm-ai-agents-and-eng-research
frontmatter.description: AI research specialist that proactively gathers latest news and developments in LLMs, AI agents, and engineering. Use for staying current with AI/ML innovations, finding actionable insights, and discovering new tools and techniques.

components.name: meta-agent
components.why_use: Reach for this agent when you need a new specialist sub-agent and want the definition generated correctly on the first try — it fetches live Anthropic docs, infers the minimal tool set, and writes the ready-to-use file. In TAC terms it is the ACT-LEARN-REUSE flywheel applied to itself: each new agent it produces becomes a reusable leverage point for future sessions.

frontmatter.name: meta-agent
frontmatter.description: Generates a new, complete Claude Code sub-agent configuration file from a user's description. Use this to create new agents. Use this Proactively when the user asks you to create a new sub agent.

components.name: work-completion-summary
components.why_use: Reach for this agent when you want the agent loop to close with a spoken status update instead of requiring the engineer to read terminal output — it keeps momentum by delivering a one-sentence completion report and a next step as audio, not text. In the hooks-mastery model it is the agent-side analogue of stop.py: the Stop hook fires TTS from the lifecycle layer, this agent fires TTS from the orchestration layer when the parent agent decides to narrate its own completion.

frontmatter.name: work-completion-summary
frontmatter.description: Proactively triggered when work is completed to provide concise audio summaries and suggest next steps. If they say 'tts' or 'tts summary' or 'audio summary' use this agent. When you prompt this agent, describe exactly what you want them to communicate to the user. Remember, this agent has no context about any questions or previous conversations between you and the user. So be sure to communicate well so they can respond to the user. Be concise, and to the point - aim for 2 sentences max.

components.name: crypto_coin_analyzer_agent_prompt
components.why_use: Reach for this prompt when you need a structured, repeatable research agent that enforces multi-source data gathering (5 tools minimum) before synthesizing — it prevents the LLM from shortcutting to hallucinated facts by making the workflow steps explicit and mandatory. Grounded in the lesson's emphasis on observable, measurable agent outputs: the required timestamp and structured output format are the LEARN step applied to financial research.

components.name: crypto_investment_plays_agent_prompt
components.why_use: Reach for this when you need a repeatable, parameterized research agent that must pull from at least MINIMUM_SOURCES before synthesizing a structured recommendation — the named variables let you tune scope without touching prompt logic. Wired as a slash command, it converts a high-cognitive-load investment research workflow into a single invocation, embodying the 'stop prompting from scratch, reuse the agent' principle that hooks mastery makes tractable at scale.

components.name: crypto_market_agent_prompt
components.why_use: Reach for this component when you need a repeatable, parameterized agent task that replaces hand-coded API integrations — invoke it with a TOP_N argument and get a structured market table without writing a single scraper. It demonstrates the ACT step of ACT-LEARN-REUSE: a fully self-contained prompt that drives agent web-search behavior toward a deterministic output contract.

components.name: crypto_movers_agent_prompt
components.why_use: Reach for this when you need a parameterized slash command that automates a structured research task and enforces a rigid output contract — the $ARGUMENTS variable and fixed markdown table show how to build composable agent prompts that stay deterministic at the output boundary. In the hooks mastery context it also demonstrates how a single command fits the ACT-LEARN-REUSE loop: invoke, capture structured output, feed downstream hooks or scripts.

components.name: crypto_news_scanner_agent_prompt
components.why_use: Reach for this component when you need a repeatable, parameterized agent to surface crypto market signals on demand — the $ARGUMENTS pattern makes it trivially composable into larger agentic pipelines without re-authoring the prompt each time. Per the lesson's ACT-LEARN-REUSE lens, this is a pre-built REUSE artifact that converts a recurring research task into a zero-code sub-agent invocation, consistent with the builder/validator team pattern shown in the repo.

components.name: crypto_price_check_agent_prompt
components.why_use: Reach for this component when you need a repeatable, parameterized agent invocation that delegates a well-scoped research task — here, live crypto price lookup — without writing any orchestration code. It embodies the hooks mastery lesson's principle that isolated, single-purpose prompts are the building block for composable agentic workflows.

components.name: macro_crypto_correlation_scanner_agent_prompt
components.why_use: Reach for this when you need a repeatable, multi-source macro+crypto research workflow that chains live data gathering (Fed policy, DXY, big-tech equities, BTC) through correlation scoring and sector sensitivity in a single slash-command invocation — turning 20 minutes of manual browser research into one structured, timestamped report. It embodies ACT-LEARN-REUSE from the hooks lesson: the fixed output schema is designed to be logged across runs, diffed, and fed back into prompt refinement cycles.

components.name: all_tools
components.why_use: Reach for this command at the start of any session where you are wiring new hooks or building agent workflows — it gives you an instant, formatted inventory of every tool your Claude Code instance can call, including MCP tools that vary by environment. It is the 'know your surface' step that prevents you from writing a PreToolUse matcher for a tool name that doesn't exist in your instance.

components.name: build
components.why_use: Reach for this command when you have a structured plan file and want the agent to implement it without improvising — it enforces plan-then-build discipline so implementation stays traceable to a documented design. In ACT-LEARN-REUSE terms, this is the ACT step: after planning produces an artifact, `/build` consumes it deterministically rather than relying on in-context memory.

frontmatter.description: Implement the plan

components.name: cook_research_only
components.why_use: Reach for this command when you need to aggregate research or analysis across multiple parallel domains in a single invocation — it eliminates sequential waiting by fanning out to N specialized sub-agents simultaneously. In the hooks mastery context this is the ACT step supercharged: one command triggers seven concurrent LEARN streams so the aggregated output arrives in the time it takes to run one.

components.name: cook
components.why_use: Reach for this command when you want to demonstrate or stress-test parallel sub-agent orchestration at scale — it fans out 7 simultaneous tasks covering research, analysis, and meta-agent generation in a single invocation. It is also the canonical example of combining live task agents with meta-agents inside one fan-out, making it the reference pattern when you need to both consume data and manufacture new agents in the same session.

components.name: crypto_research_haiku
components.why_use: Reach for this command when you need cost-efficient parallel research across multiple specialized domains — haiku models cut inference cost while parallelism eliminates sequential latency. It exemplifies the ACT-LEARN-REUSE loop: structured timestamped output directories make every run's artifacts immediately reusable for downstream analysis or prompt refinement without rerunning agents.

frontmatter.description: Execute lightweight cryptocurrency research using haiku agents

components.name: crypto_research
components.why_use: Reach for this command when a research or analysis task benefits from saturating all model tiers simultaneously — it fans 12 parallel agents across Haiku, Sonnet, and Opus in one invocation, trading token spend for speed and cross-model comparison depth. It demonstrates the lesson's core insight that custom slash commands are orchestration primitives: a single trigger wires the full parallel sub-agent pattern, structures timestamped output directories, and captures every agent's unmodified response for downstream LEARN-step analysis.

components.name: git_status
components.why_use: Reach for this command at the start of any agent session or before committing — it orients both you and the agent on exactly what has changed (diff, branch, README) in one declarative pass. It operationalizes the hooks-mastery observability principle at the git layer: you can't improve what you don't measure, and this gives you the structured measurement before the agent acts.

frontmatter.description: Understand the current state of the git repository

components.name: plan_w_team
components.why_use: Reach for plan_w_team when you need to convert an ambiguous user requirement into a validated, parallelizable team spec before any code is written — it enforces the plan-gate discipline by explicitly disallowing Task so builders structurally cannot start without a blueprint. The inline Stop hooks that machine-verify required sections (Objective, Step by Step Tasks, Team Orchestration) elevate the spec schema from soft convention to hard contract, making it the canonical first step before any builder agent team is launched.

components.name: plan
components.why_use: Reach for /plan when a task is complex enough that jumping straight to code risks expensive rework — it forces an ultrathink reasoning pass and writes a durable spec to disk that serves as both a human review checkpoint and a ready-made context artifact for downstream agent execution. In TAC terms this is the hard stop between intent and implementation, making the Big Three (context, model, prompt) cheaper to manage because the plan file becomes the single source of truth before a single line is written.

frontmatter.description: Creates a concise engineering implementation plan based on user requirements and saves it to specs directory

components.name: prime_tts
components.why_use: Reach for this command at the start of every new agent session in this repo — it front-loads the Big Three (context, model, prompt) by injecting codebase structure, README, and AI docs before any tool calls happen, collapsing the cold-start cost that kills agentic focus. It also closes the loop by handing off to the TTS summary agent, so the engineer gets an audio signal that the context is loaded and the agent is primed to build.

frontmatter.description: Load context for a new agent session by analyzing codebase structure and README

components.name: prime
components.why_use: Reach for this command at the start of any new agent session on an unfamiliar codebase — it front-loads the LEARN step by having the agent ingest structure and docs before touching anything. Without it, the agent burns context figuring out basics that a 30-second /prime would have settled upfront, degrading every subsequent tool call in the session.

frontmatter.description: Load context for a new agent session by analyzing codebase structure, documentation and README

components.name: question
components.why_use: Reach for this command when you need the agent to investigate and explain codebase structure without any risk of mutation — the allowed-tools constraint enforces read-only behavior at the harness level, not just by prompt instruction. It embodies the hooks mastery lesson's observability principle: understand what exists before deciding what to change.

frontmatter.description: Answer questions about the project structure and documentation without coding

components.name: sentient
components.why_use: Reach for this command when you need to prove that your PreToolUse hook actually blocks dangerous shell commands before trusting your hook configuration in any real workload. It is the canonical 'does my safety net catch live fire?' probe — grounded in the lesson's core point that deterministic control is only real if you can demonstrate it fires unconditionally.

frontmatter.description: Manage, organize and ships your codebase.

components.name: update_status_line
components.why_use: Reach for this command when you want to surface arbitrary context — project name, current task, debug mode — into the Claude Code status line so that long-running or parallel sessions stay self-describing at a glance. It operationalizes the ACT-LEARN-REUSE LEARN step by letting any agent or human annotate a live session with structured metadata that persists in the session JSON file, giving you the same 'measure what your agent actually did' signal that the Stop hook's transcript capture provides.

components.name: notification.py
components.why_use: Reach for this hook when running long or background agent sessions where you can't watch the terminal — it gives you ambient awareness the instant the agent pauses for permission or human input, so you don't leave it blocked for minutes. The lesson explicitly frames Notification as the 'agent needs me' interrupt signal that pairs with Stop's end-of-run announcement, completing the human-in-the-loop feedback loop at both ends of agent execution.

components.name: permission_request.py
components.why_use: Reach for this hook when you need deterministic, policy-driven permission decisions that bypass the LLM entirely — it auto-allows read-only operations and regex-matched safe bash commands so agents run without constant human interruption. It is the right tool when you want to codify your security posture once (in READ_ONLY_PATTERNS and SAFE_BASH_COMMANDS) and have every session enforce it unconditionally, which is the leverage-point model the lesson describes for PreToolUse-style blocking.

components.name: post_tool_use_failure.py
components.why_use: Reach for this hook when you need a structured, append-only audit trail of every tool invocation that failed during an agent session — failures that the LLM may silently retry or ignore. Per the lesson, the Stop hook owns transcript capture, but this hook owns the failure signal at the moment it occurs, making it the canonical artifact for the LEARN step of ACT-LEARN-REUSE when diagnosing why an agent misbehaved.

components.name: post_tool_use.py
components.why_use: Reach for this hook whenever you need a permanent, structured audit trail of every tool the agent executed — inputs and outputs alike — without any human in the loop. In TAC terms this is the LEARN step of ACT-LEARN-REUSE made automatic: every agent run accumulates a growing JSON log you can mine to tune context, model, and prompt across sessions.

components.name: pre_compact.py
components.why_use: Reach for pre_compact.py when you need a safety net at the compaction boundary — it backs up the full JSONL transcript before Claude Code's lossy context compression destroys conversation history you might need for post-run analysis. Per the lesson's LEARN principle, the structured JSON log and timestamped JSONL backup turn an otherwise invisible lifecycle event into a recoverable artifact you can feed back into prompt improvement.

components.name: pre_tool_use.py
components.why_use: Reach for this hook when you need unconditional safety enforcement that cannot be overridden by the LLM's reasoning — blocking rm -rf or .env access before the tool ever fires is a deterministic guarantee no prompt instruction can provide. It is the canonical PreToolUse implementation: intercept at the lifecycle boundary, exit non-zero to cancel, log everything so the LEARN step has a complete record of what was attempted.

components.name: session_end.py
components.why_use: Reach for session_end.py when you need automatic structured logging of every Stop-lifecycle event combined with filesystem hygiene — stale temp files and old chat.json artifacts evicted on each session boundary without any human trigger. This is the ACT-LEARN-REUSE loop made durable: the append-only JSON log gives you a queryable history of session metadata you can feed back into prompt and agent improvement cycles.

components.name: session_start.py
components.why_use: Reach for session_start.py when you need a guaranteed environmental snapshot — git branch, dirty file count, open issues — captured the instant a Claude Code session opens, before any agent tool fires. This is the LEARN step of ACT-LEARN-REUSE made automatic: structured JSON written to logs/session_start.json on every session gives you the 'starting conditions' baseline so you can diff what the agent inherited versus what it produced.

components.name: setup.py
components.why_use: Reach for this hook at session start when your agent needs a known-good environment before any tool fires — dependency checks, env var injection, and structured setup logging all happen here before the LLM ever acts. It embodies the ACT-LEARN-REUSE LEARN step at initialization time: every session writes a timestamped JSON artifact to logs/setup.json so you can audit what environment each run started with.

components.name: stop.py
components.why_use: Reach for stop.py at the exact moment an agent session ends — it's the canonical LEARN step in ACT-LEARN-REUSE, capturing the full JSONL transcript so you can analyze what your agent actually did and feed that back into prompt improvement. Wire it whenever you need zero-configuration observability on long-running or parallel-agent workloads, because the TTS+LLM completion announcement closes the feedback loop without any manual polling.

components.name: subagent_start.py
components.why_use: Reach for this hook when you're running parallel sub-agents and need real-time audio awareness the instant a task spins up — the TTS announcement fires at the SubagentStart lifecycle boundary, before the sub-agent's first tool call, giving you an immediate signal without log-polling. In the ACT-LEARN-REUSE loop it closes the observability gap at the start boundary so you can correlate when concurrent workloads begin against when they complete (SubagentStop).

components.name: subagent_stop.py
components.why_use: Reach for this hook when you are running parallel Task agents and need real-time per-agent completion signals without watching logs — it fires automatically on SubagentStop and announces each agent's finish via LLM-generated TTS so you can stay in flow. It is the sensory layer that makes high-parallelism agentic workflows tractable: you hear each sub-agent land rather than polling.

components.name: user_prompt_submit.py
components.why_use: Reach for this hook when you need structured observability at the moment of human intent — before the LLM ever sees the prompt. It implements the LEARN step of ACT-LEARN-REUSE automatically: every session's prompt history is captured to structured JSON so you can analyze what your agents were actually asked to do and improve context/prompt over time.

components.name: anth.py
components.why_use: Reach for this when a hook script needs LLM-generated natural language output — completion messages, summaries, annotations — and you want the Anthropic backend specifically. Per the lesson, the Stop hook fires a TTS completion message via an LLM call; this module is the Anthropic leg of that provider stack, keeping hook logic isolated from the project's own dependency tree.

components.name: oai.py
components.why_use: Reach for this when you need a drop-in OpenAI provider inside the hook's LLM layer — it delivers fast, optionally personalized completion messages without coupling to the Anthropic API. It is the 'O' in the Anthropic/OpenAI/Ollama fallback chain the lesson describes, letting you swap providers at the utils layer without touching any hook logic above it.

components.name: ollama.py
components.why_use: Reach for this when you need hook-generated natural language messages without cloud API dependencies — it is the local/offline LLM tier in the provider fallback stack (ElevenLabs → OpenAI → Ollama). In the LEARN step of ACT-LEARN-REUSE it enables the Stop hook to synthesize cost-free, on-device completion summaries so every agent run produces a meaningful spoken notification regardless of network or budget constraints.

components.name: task_summarizer.py
components.why_use: Reach for this when your SubagentStop hook needs to convert a raw task-completion event into an audible, human-readable announcement — it wraps a single-purpose Anthropic call inside hook infrastructure so completions narrate themselves without polling or manual inspection. In TAC terms it automates the LEARN step of ACT-LEARN-REUSE: structured completion data becomes a logged, spoken artifact that surfaces what your agents actually did.

components.name: elevenlabs_tts.py
components.why_use: Reach for this when a Stop or Notification hook needs high-quality, low-latency voice output to close the human feedback loop — it sits at the top of the ElevenLabs → OpenAI → pyttsx3 fallback stack and is the preferred provider when an API key is available. In the ACT-LEARN-REUSE cycle this is the sensory output of the LEARN step: you hear agent completion rather than polling a log.

components.name: openai_tts.py
components.why_use: Reach for this when your Stop or Notification hooks need to announce agent completion via voice and you want OpenAI's streaming TTS quality over the pyttsx3 fallback — it slots into the ElevenLabs → OpenAI → pyttsx3 provider chain so you hear the agent finish rather than polling a terminal. It embodies the LEARN step of ACT-LEARN-REUSE with a sensory channel: structured logs tell you what happened, TTS tells you when to look.

components.name: pyttsx3_tts.py
components.why_use: Reach for this when your hook notification stack must work in air-gapped, offline, or zero-API-key environments — it is the last-resort fallback in the ElevenLabs → OpenAI → pyttsx3 provider chain that fires when a Stop or SubagentStop event completes. Because hooks survive into `claude -p` headless mode, you need a TTS tier that never fails due to missing credentials; pyttsx3 gives you that guarantee so the observability signal always lands.

components.name: tts_queue.py
components.why_use: Reach for tts_queue.py whenever parallel sub-agents each fire TTS announcements on completion — without a cross-process mutex, simultaneous SubagentStop events will overlap audio and render all announcements unintelligible. It is the serialization primitive that makes the SubagentStop → TTS pipeline reliable at scale, embodying the lesson's core point that parallel agents require deterministic coordination your code controls, not the LLM.

components.name: ruff_validator.py
components.why_use: Reach for this component when you need deterministic code-quality enforcement inside the agent loop — the LLM wrote a Python file, but you don't trust it to lint-clean its own output, so this hook intercepts the PostToolUse event and blocks the action with a reason that forces a retry before the agent moves on. As the lesson emphasizes, hooks give you unconditional control that the model cannot override; pairing a validator here with the PreToolUse safety block creates a full quality perimeter around every file write.

components.name: ty_validator.py
components.why_use: Reach for ty_validator when you want the agent to self-correct type errors immediately after writing Python — it fires as a PostToolUse hook and blocks the tool result until `uvx ty check` passes, making type safety a hard gate rather than a suggestion. This is the ACT-LEARN loop made automatic: the agent writes code, the hook measures it, and the block+retry forces improvement before the next step.

components.name: validate_file_contains.py
components.why_use: Reach for this when you need the agent to prove its artifact meets a structural contract before it's allowed to stop — the imperative error messages ('Do not stop until all required sections are present') turn a passive check into a self-correcting repair loop with zero human involvement. In TAC terms it automates the LEARN step of ACT-LEARN-REUSE: every Stop event either confirms output quality or re-queues the agent with a precise, actionable repair instruction.

components.name: validate_new_file.py
components.why_use: Reach for this component when you need a hard postcondition on file creation — it converts a git-status filesystem check into a binary exit code that blocks the agent from proceeding if the expected artifact never materialized. It closes the ACT-LEARN loop described in the hooks mastery lesson: the structured error message with 'Do not stop until the file has been created' turns a failed validation into an automatic retry signal rather than a silent hallucinated success.

components.name: Bullet Points
components.why_use: Reach for this output-style when you need agent responses formatted for rapid human triage — bullet hierarchy enforces scanability over narrative, which matters when reviewing multi-step plans, checking mid-loop agent output, or reading Stop-hook transcript summaries without post-processing. In the hooks-mastery context, injecting this style means every session summary the Stop hook captures arrives pre-structured and skimmable with zero extra tooling.

frontmatter.name: Bullet Points
frontmatter.description: Hierarchical bullet points for quick scanning

components.name: GenUI
components.why_use: Reach for GenUI when you want every agent response to produce a human-readable, browser-rendered artifact instead of raw text — especially during the LEARN step of ACT-LEARN-REUSE where reviewing agent output visually accelerates iteration. It pairs naturally with the hooks observability pattern from this lesson: just as PostToolUse logs structured JSON for machine consumption, GenUI logs structured HTML for human consumption.

frontmatter.name: GenUI
frontmatter.description: Generative UI with embedded modern styling

components.name: HTML Structured
components.why_use: Reach for this output-style when your agent pipeline needs to hand its results to a downstream renderer, parser, or log aggregator — the semantic HTML5 structure plus data-* attributes make tool outputs machine-readable without a JSON extraction step. In the hooks-mastery lesson context, this pairs naturally with the PostToolUse log architecture: structured HTML responses are as easy to snapshot and analyze as JSON, feeding directly into the ACT-LEARN-REUSE loop.

frontmatter.name: HTML Structured
frontmatter.description: Clean semantic HTML with proper structure

components.name: Markdown Focused
components.why_use: Reach for this when you need Claude's output to be consistently structured for human consumption in markdown-rendering environments — terminals, IDEs, web UIs. In the hooks context, analysis artifacts from the Stop hook (transcript summaries, log reports) become scannable and reusable when they follow a defined formatting contract, directly supporting the LEARN phase of ACT-LEARN-REUSE.

frontmatter.name: Markdown Focused
frontmatter.description: Full markdown features for maximum readability

components.name: Table Based
components.why_use: Reach for this output-style when your agent needs to surface comparison, configuration, or multi-step data in a scannable format — the Stop hook's transcript capture and PostToolUse logs are exactly the kind of structured output that benefits from table organization. Wire it into your meta-prompt layer to enforce consistent LLM responses across all agents in a team, since readable agent output is a prerequisite for the LEARN step in ACT-LEARN-REUSE.

frontmatter.name: Table Based
frontmatter.description: Markdown tables for better organization and scanning

components.name: TTS Summary
components.why_use: Reach for this output style when you want personalized audio feedback at the end of every agent response — it turns silent task completions into spoken confirmations that let you stay off-screen during long runs. It is the agent-side complement to the Stop/PostToolUse hooks: where those fire TTS from the harness, this output style fires TTS from within the agent response itself, giving you two independent announcement layers.

frontmatter.name: TTS Summary
frontmatter.description: Audio task completion announcements with TTS

components.name: Ultra Concise
components.why_use: Reach for this when agent verbosity is actively slowing you down — focused build sprints, tight debug loops, or any session where explanation overhead exceeds its value. The lesson's 'Big Three' (context, model, prompt) principle applies here: this is a prompt-layer lever that reduces noise in every response without touching the model or tool configuration.

frontmatter.name: Ultra Concise
frontmatter.description: Minimal words maximum speed direct actions

components.name: YAML Structured
components.why_use: Reach for this output style when downstream hooks or scripts need to parse agent responses programmatically — YAML's strict schema turns the LLM's non-deterministic prose into a machine-readable contract that PostToolUse log processing and ACT-LEARN-REUSE analysis can consume deterministically. It is the prompt-layer complement to structured JSON logs: same discipline, applied to the response side of the agent loop.

frontmatter.name: YAML Structured
