components.name: settings.json
components.why_use: Reach for settings.json when you need deterministic, LLM-bypassing control over what your agent is allowed to execute and which scripts intercept each lifecycle event — it is the single source of truth that wires hook scripts to PreToolUse/PostToolUse/Stop events and enforces the permissions sandbox. This is the first file to author when standing up a new hooks-based observability or safety layer, because every other hook script is inert until this manifest activates it.

components.name: README
components.why_use: Reach for this when you need to quickly orient to which AI doc file covers a specific hooks lifecycle event, subagent wiring, or status line config — it collapses four URL-backed references into a single lookup. In the lesson context it is the entry point for the LEARN step of ACT-LEARN-REUSE: before authoring or debugging any hook script, this index tells you exactly which doc to open.

components.name: README
components.why_use: Reach for this README when onboarding to the hooks system or auditing which lifecycle events are available — it is the authoritative map of all 13 hook events with payload shapes, flow control exit codes, and settings.json wiring syntax before you write a single line of code. In ACT-LEARN-REUSE terms this is the canonical LEARN artifact: study it first, then instrument the specific PreToolUse or Stop hooks your workload needs.

components.name: create-worktree-subagent
components.why_use: Reach for this agent when you need to spin up a parallel git worktree via explicit subagent delegation — the strict trigger guard ('only when user says subagent') keeps it from firing opportunistically and makes human intent the gate. In the lesson's framing of scale-compute-to-scale-impact, worktrees are the local analogue to E2B sandboxes: isolated environments where parallel agents can each own a branch without stepping on each other.

frontmatter.name: create-worktree-subagent
frontmatter.description: Use when the user explicitly asks for a SUBAGENT to create a worktree. If the user does not mention "subagent" or explicitly request subagent delegation, do NOT trigger this. Only use when user says things like "use a subagent to create a worktree" or "delegate worktree creation to a subagent". Creates isolated git worktrees with parallel-running configuration.
frontmatter.tools: SlashCommand, Bash, Read, Write, Edit, Glob, Grep

components.name: docs-scraper
components.why_use: Reach for docs-scraper whenever you need to populate the Context leg of Core Four before heavier agents start work — it converts any URL into a clean, offline-ready markdown file in one shot so downstream agents reason over local docs rather than making repeated live fetches. In a multi-agent setup it is the canonical lightweight Haiku subagent to invoke proactively during the knowledge-acquisition phase, keeping expensive orchestrator context windows free of raw scrape noise.

frontmatter.name: docs-scraper
frontmatter.description: Documentation scraping specialist. Use proactively to fetch and save documentation from URLs as properly formatted markdown files.

components.name: fetch-docs-haiku45
components.why_use: Reach for this agent when an orchestrator needs to retrieve and persist external documentation at minimum token cost — Haiku 4.5 handles pure I/O retrieval without burning Sonnet/Opus budget on a task that requires no reasoning. Its explicit model pin and benchmarking framing make it the right pick when you need a reproducible, cost-bounded baseline to compare against higher-tier retrieval agents, which maps directly to the Core Four principle of choosing the right model for the right task.

frontmatter.name: fetch-docs-haiku45
frontmatter.description: Fetch and save documentation from URLs using Haiku 4.5 model. Use for benchmarking documentation retrieval tasks.

components.name: fetch-docs-sonnet45
components.why_use: Reach for this agent when you need to pull complete documentation from a URL and persist it verbatim to disk as a single autonomous step — no summarization, no truncation. The explicit Sonnet 4.5 model pin makes it the reference side of a benchmark pair; use it alongside a parallel agent pinned to a newer model to measure retrieval quality or latency deltas across model generations.

frontmatter.name: fetch-docs-sonnet45
frontmatter.description: Fetch and save documentation from URLs using Sonnet 4.5 model. Use for benchmarking documentation retrieval tasks.

components.name: meta-agent
components.why_use: Reach for meta-agent when you need to mint a new sub-agent from a natural-language description without hand-authoring frontmatter, tool lists, or system prompts — it fetches live Anthropic docs, infers the minimal tool set, and writes the ready-to-run file in one shot. In the lesson's multi-agent orchestration context, this is the fastest on-ramp to growing your agent team: describe the role, get the agent, drop it into the swarm.

frontmatter.name: meta-agent
frontmatter.description: Generates a new, complete Claude Code sub-agent configuration file from a user's description. Use this to create new agents. Use this Proactively when the user asks you to create a new sub agent.

components.name: scout-report-suggest-fast
components.why_use: Reach for this agent when you need rapid, safe codebase analysis before committing to a fix — it deliberately limits itself to Read/Glob/Grep so it cannot cause side effects in a parallel multi-agent swarm. In the orchestration pattern IDD demonstrates, a scout like this is the natural first subagent: surface exact file paths and line numbers, then hand the structured report to a write-capable executor.

frontmatter.name: scout-report-suggest-fast
frontmatter.description: Use proactively to quickly scout codebase issues, identify problem locations, and suggest resolutions. Specialist for read-only analysis and reporting without making changes.

components.name: scout-report-suggest
components.why_use: Reach for scout-report-suggest when you need a zero-side-effect diagnostic pass before any fix agent touches a file — it surfaces exact paths, line numbers, and root causes so the downstream executor walks in with a verified target list rather than assumptions. In the lesson's multi-agent orchestration model, it slots cleanly as the read-only analyst half of a builder+validator split, producing observable, auditable reports that feed directly into the orchestration pipeline without polluting the write surface.

frontmatter.name: scout-report-suggest
frontmatter.description: Use proactively to scout codebase issues, identify problem locations, and suggest resolutions. Specialist for read-only analysis and reporting without making changes.

components.name: find_and_summarize
components.why_use: Reach for this command when you need a structured, reproducible snapshot of a subsystem before starting a build or orchestration task — it compresses codebase understanding into a single YAML artifact without polluting the agent's context with ad-hoc file reads. In the lesson's multi-agent context, it is exactly the kind of drop-in reusable primitive (Tactic #2) that primes an orchestrator's context window before fanning work out to subagents.

frontmatter.description: Finds and summarizes specific files in the codebase and saves the summary to app_docs directory

components.name: load_ai_docs
components.why_use: Reach for this command when you need to compare model-specific subagent performance against a fixed documentation-retrieval and QA benchmark — it wires the Task tool, file I/O, and structured question-answering into a single repeatable harness. In TAC terms it operationalizes tactic/6 and tactic/7 together: spawn named fetch-agents per model/run, collect their output, and surface pass/fail telemetry in a consistent report format that can be diffed across runs.

frontmatter.description: Fetch and save AI documentation using model-specific subagents for benchmarking

components.name: plan_new_feature
components.why_use: Reach for this command when you need a deeply-reasoned implementation spec before any code is written — it enforces the 'plan not build' discipline at the prompt level so an engineer can validate strategy before committing compute or spawning builder agents. In the IDD multi-agent orchestration model, it is the upstream artifact producer: its output spec becomes the reliable blueprint that feeds builder agents while eliminating premature implementation drift.

frontmatter.description: Creates a concise engineering implementation plan based on user requirements and saves it to specs directory

components.name: build
components.why_use: Reach for /build when you have a structured plan artifact on disk and want an agent to autonomously implement it end-to-end — it is the execution half of a plan→build agentic loop and pairs directly with /plan_w_team. In the lesson's multi-agent setup, this command is what a builder-role subagent runs: it scales compute to scale impact by delegating full codebase implementation to an agent that ultrathinks through the plan before touching a single file.

frontmatter.description: Build the codebase based on the plan

components.name: convert_paths_absolute
components.why_use: Reach for this command when onboarding a project into the multi-agent observability grid: hook scripts must resolve at runtime regardless of CWD, so relative paths in settings.json are latent failure points. It is also the right tool after cloning or moving the repo — one invocation hardens every command script path before the first agent session starts.

frontmatter.description: Converts relative paths in .claude/settings.json command scripts to absolute paths

components.name: create_worktree_prompt
components.why_use: Reach for this command when you need to run multiple independent instances of the observability system simultaneously — each with its own ports, database, and hook configuration — without any manual environment wiring. In the lesson's framing of 'scale compute to scale impact,' this command is the local analogue to E2B sandboxes: it creates an isolated compute substrate per branch so parallel agents never collide.

components.name: list_worktrees_prompt
components.why_use: Reach for this command when running a parallel multi-agent worktree setup and you need an instant snapshot of which branches are provisioned, how they are configured, and whether their servers and clients are alive. In the context of multi-agent observability, it is the human-facing analog to the dashboard—giving the orchestrating engineer ground truth about the compute substrate before spawning or debugging agents.

frontmatter.description: List all git worktrees with their configuration and status

components.name: load_ai_docs
components.why_use: Reach for this command at session start when your agents need current, local copies of external AI docs — it handles staleness checks, parallel scraping, and caching in one shot so every downstream agent starts with grounded context rather than raw URLs. In TAC terms this is pure Tactic #1 context-engineering: instead of sending agents to the web mid-task, you front-load the Context pillar of the Core Four once and reuse it across the swarm.

frontmatter.description: Load documentation from their respective websites into local markdown files our agents can use as context.
frontmatter.allowed-tools: Task, WebFetch, Write, Edit, Bash(ls*), mcp__firecrawl-mcp__firecrawl_scrape

components.name: plan_w_team
components.why_use: Reach for this command when a task is complex enough that a single agent will thrash — it converts a raw user requirement into a structured multi-agent execution blueprint (team composition, task dependencies, parallel vs. sequential decisions) before any code is written. Grounded in the 'systems of trust' principle from Tactic #6: the output is an auditable spec in specs/ that humans review before the team runs, making orchestration intentional rather than emergent.

components.name: prime
components.why_use: Reach for /prime at the start of any new session or before spawning subagents to front-load the codebase map into the context window — it directly serves the context pillar of Core Four and prevents agents from operating on an empty or stale mental model. In the multi-agent orchestration pattern this repo demonstrates, priming is the zero-cost ritual that keeps every spawned agent oriented without burning tokens on redundant discovery mid-task.

components.name: quick-plan
components.why_use: Reach for quick-plan when a requirement is complex enough to warrant a blueprint before any code is written — the explicit ultrathink directive front-loads deep reasoning into the spec artifact rather than mid-implementation, which is the Core Four 'prompt' lever applied at planning time. In the multi-agent orchestration model from this lesson, quick-plan is the spec-generation handoff that gives builder agents (like builder.md) a reliable, structured artifact instead of an ad-hoc freeform prompt.

frontmatter.allowed-tools: Read, Write, Edit, Glob, Grep, MultiEdit
frontmatter.description: Creates a concise engineering implementation plan based on user requirements and saves it to specs directory

components.name: remove_worktree_prompt
components.why_use: Reach for this command at the end of a parallel worktree workstream when you need to atomically tear down an agent's isolated environment — stopping live services, pruning the directory, and deleting the branch in one shot. In the IDD multi-agent orchestration pattern, this mirrors the deliberate forced teardown (team_delete) that resets context and prevents orphaned processes or branches from accumulating across long-running swarm sessions.

frontmatter.description: Remove a git worktree, delete its branch, and stop its running services

components.name: start
components.why_use: Reach for this command at the beginning of any multi-agent session where you need the full observability pipeline running before agents start emitting hook events — it bootstraps the Bun server and Vue dashboard so no telemetry is lost. IDD's repo treats this as the mandatory precondition to the hooks → HTTP → SQLite → WebSocket → dashboard flow described in the lesson.

components.name: t_metaprompt_workflow
components.why_use: Reach for this command when you need to manufacture a new slash command from a one-line intent — it eliminates hand-authoring frontmatter, sections, and argument wiring by encoding the entire format as a template the agent fills in. It is the canonical expression of ACT-LEARN-REUSE: once a workflow is worth repeating, this command crystallizes it into a reusable primitive that any agent or engineer can invoke.

frontmatter.allowed-tools: Write, Edit, WebFetch, Task, mcp__firecrawl-mcp__firecrawl_scrape, Fetch
frontmatter.description: Create a new prompt

components.name: hitl_example.py
components.why_use: Reach for this component when an agent encounters a decision point that carries real risk or ambiguity — destructive operations, style choices, environment-specific unknowns — and you need human judgment before proceeding rather than autonomous inference. In the lesson's framing of 'systems of trust,' HITL is the safety valve that lets you scale agentic compute while keeping a human in the critical path at exactly the right moments.

components.name: notification.py
components.why_use: Reach for notification.py when your multi-agent workflow has a human-in-the-loop checkpoint and the engineer is not actively watching the terminal — it converts the agent's permission_prompt or idle_prompt pause into an audio interrupt so human latency never becomes pipeline latency. Tactic #7 is the hook-driven feedback loop; this component extends that loop into the physical room, making the agent's blocked state audible rather than just visible on the dashboard.

components.name: permission_request.py
components.why_use: Reach for this hook when you need a permanent, queryable audit trail of every permission_request event without ever interrupting agent flow — it appends structured JSON to per-session log files and always exits 0. In IDD's observability pipeline, passive loggers like this are what make the invisible visible across multi-agent swarms; the dashboard and downstream analytics depend on these silent per-session breadcrumbs.

components.name: post_tool_use_failure.py
components.why_use: Reach for this hook whenever you need a durable, session-scoped failure audit trail for every tool invocation that errors in a multi-agent swarm — the lesson's observability pipeline is only trustworthy if the failure path is captured with the same fidelity as the success path. It is the minimum viable safety net that lets you diagnose silent agent failures post-hoc without instrumenting individual agent prompts.

components.name: post_tool_use.py
components.why_use: Reach for post_tool_use.py when you need passive, zero-risk telemetry on every tool invocation without any chance of blocking agent execution — it always exits 0 and swallows all exceptions. In this repo it is the canonical Tactic #7 implementation: capture rich metadata (MCP server, tool name, session ID, is_mcp_tool flag) after each tool call and append it to a per-session JSON log so the dashboard and any post-hoc analysis have a complete, unbroken audit trail.

components.name: pre_compact.py
components.why_use: Reach for this hook whenever you need a safety net around Claude Code's context compaction — it fires automatically at the PreCompact lifecycle event, backs up the full transcript JSONL before any tokens are dropped, and logs the trigger + custom instructions so you can reconstruct what the agent knew before the reset. In long-running multi-agent sessions (like the swarm demo in the lesson), losing transcript history silently is a trust-breaker; this hook makes compaction a visible, recoverable event rather than an invisible one.

components.name: pre_tool_use.py
components.why_use: Reach for this hook whenever you need an autonomous safety layer between the agent and destructive filesystem operations — it intercepts every Bash tool call before execution and hard-blocks rm -rf patterns that fall outside an explicit allowlist, making dangerous side-effects structurally impossible rather than prompt-dependent. In the lesson's multi-agent context, where a swarm of subagents each carry isolated context windows and no shared memory, this PreToolUse guard is the one enforcement point that survives prompt drift and scales across every agent in the team without per-agent configuration.

components.name: send_event.py
components.why_use: Reach for send_event.py whenever you need zero-code observability across a Claude Code swarm — drop it into .claude/hooks/ and every lifecycle event (PreToolUse, SubagentStart, Stop, etc.) is automatically captured, enriched with model and transcript metadata, and forwarded to your pipeline without touching agent logic. It is the canonical hook-to-HTTP relay IDD built to make the invisible visible, directly embodying Tactic #7's principle that structured observability is the prerequisite for trusting and scaling multi-agent systems.

components.name: session_end.py
components.why_use: Reach for session_end.py when you need passive, zero-config telemetry at agent teardown — it auto-captures session ID, end reason, transcript path, and message count the moment a session closes, feeding the observability pipeline IDD demonstrates in Tactic #7. Without a hook at this lifecycle boundary, you lose the only moment where per-session analytics (message volume, end reason distribution) can be recorded without polling or replaying transcripts after the fact.

components.name: session_start.py
components.why_use: Reach for session_start.py when you need a zero-touch entry point to capture agent identity (model, agent_type, source) and environment state (git branch, dirty-file count) the moment a session opens — before any tool fires. In the Tactic #7 observability stack this hook is the swimlane anchor: without it the dashboard cannot color-code per-agent timelines or correlate tool events back to the originating session.

components.name: stop.py
components.why_use: Reach for stop.py whenever you need post-session telemetry, human-audible completion signals, or a guard against infinite hook loops — it fires automatically on every Claude Code session end without any human trigger. In the multi-agent observability lesson, it is the canonical example of closing the feedback loop: the agent finishes, the hook POSTs the event, speaks a TTS message, and the dashboard marks the swimlane complete.

components.name: subagent_start.py
components.why_use: Reach for this hook when you need passive, zero-configuration subagent spawn tracking in a multi-agent swarm — it fires automatically on every SubagentStart event and appends a full payload snapshot to a per-session log file with no side effects. In the context of IDD's observability pipeline, it is the filesystem-layer half of the 'make the invisible visible' pattern: local durable logs that survive even if the Bun WebSocket server is down.

components.name: subagent_stop.py
components.why_use: Reach for subagent_stop.py when you need audible confirmation that a swarm member has finished — critical in tmux multi-pane sessions where you cannot watch every pane simultaneously. It closes Tactic #7's observability loop at the subagent boundary by pairing the SubagentStop lifecycle event with TTS announcement, so you know the moment off-device compute finishes without polling.

components.name: test_hitl.py
components.why_use: Reach for test_hitl.py when you need to smoke-test your Human-In-The-Loop permission gate before wiring it into a live agent workflow — it simulates a dangerous command scenario and blocks until a human approves or denies via the dashboard. Per the lesson's emphasis on 'building systems of trust with our agents,' running this script first confirms the full HITL pipeline (hook → HTTP → WebSocket → dashboard → response) is healthy before autonomous agents depend on it.

components.name: user_prompt_submit.py
components.why_use: Reach for this hook when your multi-agent swarm needs durable session identity across all prompts — it persists each user prompt into a per-session JSON store and optionally assigns human-readable names to agents via LLM, giving your observability pipeline the identity layer Tactic #7 depends on. Without it, dashboard swimlanes remain UUID-keyed; with it, every agent in the swarm becomes a named actor you can trace across the event timeline.

components.name: constants.py
components.why_use: Reach for this utility when building a multi-hook observability pipeline where every hook script must write logs to the same session-scoped filesystem layout without coordination overhead. It is the single source of truth for LOG_BASE_DIR, so swapping the log root via CLAUDE_HOOKS_LOG_DIR propagates to all 12 event handlers at once — exactly the kind of drop-in infrastructure IDD describes when adding the .claude/ directory to any project to join the observability grid.

components.name: hitl.py
components.why_use: Reach for HITLRequest when an autonomous hook needs to pause execution and get explicit human approval, a choice, or an answer before continuing — the canonical case is a PreToolUse hook that intercepts a dangerous command and refuses to unblock until the engineer responds via the observability dashboard. IDD's framing of 'systems of trust with our agents' demands this: observability alone shows what happened, HITL lets you gate what happens next.

components.name: anth.py
components.why_use: Reach for this component when a hook needs to cross the pure-signal boundary and produce natural-language intelligence — dynamic completion messages, tool-input summaries, or any spot where a hard-coded string would be worse than a model-generated one. In IDD's Core Four framing this IS the Model pillar inside the hook layer: it wires the fastest available Haiku directly into zero-touch lifecycle events so observability gains reasoning without adding human latency.

components.name: oai.py
components.why_use: Reach for this when a hook needs to emit natural-language feedback (completion messages, summaries, TTS payloads) instead of hardcoded strings — it keeps the LLM call isolated from hook orchestration logic. In the observability pipeline described in the lesson, enriching stop/notification events with generated prose is exactly where this utility sits; it lets hooks stay thin while the LLM layer stays swappable.

components.name: model_extractor.py
components.why_use: Reach for this utility whenever a hook script needs to surface which Claude model is active for the current session — model identity is one of the Core Four, and knowing it at event-time lets you annotate, route, or filter observability payloads by model tier across a swarm. In a multi-agent setup where Opus, Sonnet, and Haiku may run concurrently in separate panes, this extractor gives each hook the session-scoped model name from the JSONL transcript without redundant I/O, backed by an optional TTL cache.

components.name: summarizer.py
components.why_use: Reach for this component when your observability dashboard needs human-readable narration of raw hook payloads rather than dumping JSON at engineers — it applies Tactic #7 by having the model itself interpret its own tool calls in real time. IDD's lesson frames the hooks-to-dashboard pipeline as 'making the invisible visible'; this utility is the LLM layer that turns opaque payloads into 15-word engineer-legible lines that can appear in the Vue swimlane view.

components.name: elevenlabs_tts.py
components.why_use: Reach for this when your hook observability pipeline needs to surface agent events as audio signals — specifically when notification.py fires on permission_prompt or idle_prompt and you need the engineer's eyes back on the terminal without them watching a dashboard. As IDD frames it: building systems of trust with agents means making the invisible visible; this script extends that principle from the Vue swimlane dashboard into the auditory channel, so a permission block or idle stall announces itself instead of silently stalling compute.

components.name: openai_tts.py
components.why_use: Reach for this component when you want the hook observability pipeline to surface human-attention events—permission prompts, idle waits—as spoken audio rather than silent dashboard entries; it turns Tactic 7's invisible hook traffic into a sensory interrupt that keeps an engineer informed without requiring eyes on a screen. It is the audio layer of the `notification.py` hook and belongs in any multi-agent setup where the operator is away from the dashboard but needs immediate awareness of agent state changes.

components.name: pyttsx3_tts.py
components.why_use: Reach for this component when you need zero-dependency, offline audio feedback from a hook — specifically inside the notification hook where the agent needs to surface permission prompts or idle states to a human without requiring network access or an API key. In the IDD observability stack, TTS is the last-mile output that makes the invisible visible in a human-perceptible way, complementing the Vue dashboard's visual swimlanes with an audible signal.

components.name: validate_file_contains.py
components.why_use: Reach for this hook when you need to enforce structural contracts on agent-produced files — e.g., guaranteeing that a spec written during a /plan_w_team run contains all required sections before the session closes. It operationalizes Tactic #7's principle of making agent behavior visible and correctable by turning a silent omission into an explicit, blocking exit-2 that surfaces the gap immediately.

components.name: validate_new_file.py
components.why_use: Reach for this when you need a hard delivery contract on a subagent: the Stop hook's exit-2 path physically prevents the agent from terminating until the required file exists, so the orchestrator can trust the artifact is there rather than just take the agent's word for it. In the lesson's multi-agent orchestration context this is the mechanism behind 'systems of trust' — the validator is wired into the stop-hook chain of the plan_w_team workflow so no agent in the swarm can silently declare done without proof of output.

components.name: Bullet Points
components.why_use: Reach for this component whenever an agent's output will be consumed by humans who need to scan quickly — code reviews, task breakdowns, observability summaries — because it enforces hierarchical bullet discipline that keeps dense agentic output readable at a glance. In the multi-agent orchestration context IDD demonstrates, where a dashboard surfaces dozens of concurrent tool events, consistent output formatting is as important as the data itself for maintaining situational awareness.

frontmatter.name: Bullet Points
frontmatter.description: Hierarchical bullet points for quick scanning

components.name: GenUI
components.why_use: Reach for this output-style when you want every agent response to land as an immediately-renderable, self-contained HTML artefact instead of plain text — no external deps, no follow-up 'open in browser' step. In the multi-agent observability context Dan demonstrates, pairing GenUI with hook dashboards means a subagent can surface structured results (build reports, diff summaries, validation tables) as visual documents that the orchestrator or human can inspect without leaving the terminal flow.

frontmatter.name: GenUI
frontmatter.description: Generative UI with embedded modern styling

components.name: HTML Structured
components.why_use: Reach for this component when an agent's output must be consumed by a downstream renderer, parser, or dashboard — the semantic HTML contract makes tool call results, file diffs, and status messages machine-readable without a separate serialization step. In the observability context from the lesson, structured output styles let the Vue client or any WebSocket consumer parse agent responses without brittle regex; the `data-*` attributes carry the same metadata that hook payloads capture at the event level.

frontmatter.name: HTML Structured
frontmatter.description: Clean semantic HTML with proper structure

components.name: Markdown Focused
components.why_use: Reach for this output style when you want every agent in an orchestration swarm to produce structured, scannable responses that are easy to review across a multi-agent observability dashboard — the formatting contract is loaded once and inherited by all downstream agents with zero per-call overhead. IDD's Core Four principle applies directly: this file engineers the 'prompt' dimension so the context, model, and tools can stay focused on the task instead of rediscovering formatting rules each turn.

frontmatter.name: Markdown Focused
frontmatter.description: Full markdown features for maximum readability

components.name: observable-tools-diffs-tts
components.why_use: Drop this output style into any Claude Code project when you need a human-readable audit trail of every agent action — git diffs surface exactly what changed, ordered tool calls expose the reasoning chain, and TTS keeps Dan (or any named user) informed without watching the terminal. It is the output-layer complement to the hook-driven observability pipeline demonstrated in this lesson: hooks capture the machine-level event stream, this style narrates the human-facing summary.

components.name: observable-tools-diffs
components.why_use: Reach for this output style when you are in-loop and need agent actions auditable without spinning up a live hook dashboard — it surfaces every tool call in TypeScript interface syntax and every code change as a scoped git diff directly in the response stream. In the lesson's hook-driven observability stack this is the human-readable complement to the WebSocket pipeline: where hooks capture machine-readable events for the Vue swimlane view, this style delivers the same signal inline so a reviewer can verify diffs without leaving the chat.

components.name: Table Based
components.why_use: Reach for this output style when agents need to deliver structured, scannable results that orchestrators, validators, or humans can parse at a glance — particularly in multi-agent pipelines where a downstream agent must consume a subagent's findings without re-reading prose. In the Core Four frame, shaping output format is context engineering: a table-first style reduces cognitive load on whatever reads the agent's work next, making the whole pipeline faster and more reliable.

frontmatter.name: Table Based
frontmatter.description: Markdown tables for better organization and scanning

components.name: TTS Summary
components.why_use: Reach for this when running long or parallel agent sessions where you want ambient audio awareness of completions without staying glued to the terminal — it turns every agent response into a spoken announcement so you can context-switch freely and still know when tasks finish. In IDD's Tactic #7 framing, this complements the visual hook dashboard by adding a second sensory channel: hooks surface what agents did to a UI; this style announces it to the human out loud.

frontmatter.name: TTS Summary
frontmatter.description: Audio task completion announcements with TTS

components.name: TTS Summary
components.why_use: Reach for this output style when you want Claude Code to proactively announce task completions via TTS and surface a chronological tool-call trace at the end of every response — turning Claude's output channel into a lightweight audit trail without requiring hook infrastructure. In the lesson context, it complements the hook-driven observability dashboard by adding a human-audible signal layer that keeps the engineer aware of agent activity across long autonomous sessions, mapping directly to Tactic #7's goal of making the invisible visible.

frontmatter.name: TTS Summary
frontmatter.description: Audio task completion announcements with TTS

components.name: Ultra Concise
components.why_use: Reach for this when multi-agent token overhead is degrading signal clarity — concise agent output reduces observability dashboard noise and speeds up orchestrator parsing of subagent results. In IDD's hook pipeline, where every tool call across every agent streams live to a Vue swimlane view, verbose agent chatter is a direct throughput tax on the whole swarm.

frontmatter.name: Ultra Concise
frontmatter.description: Minimal words maximum speed direct actions

components.name: YAML Structured
components.why_use: Reach for this when agent outputs must be machine-parseable downstream — feeding observability pipelines, inter-agent handoffs, or structured logs without regex scraping. In a multi-agent swarm where hooks capture every tool event, enforcing YAML at the output layer makes post-processing trivial and eliminates brittle prose parsing.

frontmatter.name: YAML Structured
frontmatter.description: Structured YAML with hierarchical key value pairs

components.name: settings.json
components.why_use: Reach for this settings.json when you want to drop the full observability pipeline into any project — every Claude Code lifecycle event is intercepted, enriched, and forwarded to the telemetry server with zero per-project code changes required beyond copying the .claude/ directory. It also gates experimental agent teams via env var, making it the single declarative knob that simultaneously unlocks multi-agent orchestration and wires the observability harness that makes that orchestration legible.

components.name: create-worktree-skill
components.why_use: Reach for this skill when you need parallel, branch-isolated development environments on the local machine — the same 'isolated compute substrate' pattern IDD demonstrates with E2B sandboxes, but scoped to a single developer's workstation. It packages the entire worktree setup ceremony (ports, env files, deps, service start) into a single reusable invocation, making it a drop-in primitive for any multi-branch workflow.

frontmatter.name: create-worktree-skill
frontmatter.description: Use when the user explicitly asks for a SKILL to create a worktree. If the user does not mention "skill" or explicitly request skill invocation, do NOT trigger this. Only use when user says things like "use a skill to create a worktree" or "invoke the worktree skill". Creates isolated git worktrees with parallel-running configuration.
frontmatter.allowed-tools: SlashCommand, Bash, Read, Write, Edit, Glob, Grep

components.name: Create New Skills
components.why_use: Reach for this skill whenever you want to encode hard-won domain knowledge into a first-class reusable primitive that any teammate (or subagent) can invoke by name — it is the canonical entry point for extending Claude's skill library. In the lesson context, IDD frames Skills as the mechanism behind Tactic #2 (ACT-LEARN-REUSE): you run something once, then package it so the next agent inherits the expertise instead of reinventing it.

frontmatter.name: Create New Skills
frontmatter.description: Creates new Agent Skills for Claude Code following best practices and documentation. Use when the user wants to create a new skill, extend Claude's capabilities, or package domain expertise into a reusable skill.

components.name: Video Processor
components.why_use: Reach for this skill when an agentic workflow needs to ingest, convert, or transcribe video assets without leaving the Claude Code context — it packages FFmpeg and Whisper behind a clean CLI so the agent can treat media processing as a single tool call. In the lesson context this is the enabling primitive that lets any observability repo close the loop on its own content: record a session, extract audio, and transcribe it back into knowledge without leaving the agentic loop.

frontmatter.name: Video Processor
frontmatter.description: Process video files with audio extraction, format conversion (mp4, webm), and Whisper transcription. Use when user mentions video conversion, audio extraction, transcription, mp4, webm, ffmpeg, or whisper transcription.

components.name: worktree-manager-skill
components.why_use: Reach for this skill when an engineer needs parallel development environments without manual overhead — it enforces slash-command discipline (no raw git commands, no manual port wiring) so parallel branches or agent swarms stay cleanly isolated. In the lesson's orchestration model, where each subagent gets its own context window and tmux pane, worktrees are the local-environment analog: isolated state, reproducible teardown, zero cross-contamination.

frontmatter.name: worktree-manager-skill
frontmatter.description: Comprehensive git worktree management. Use when the user wants to create, remove, list, or manage worktrees. Handles all worktree operations including creation, deletion, and status checking.
frontmatter.allowed-tools: SlashCommand, Bash, Read, Write, Edit, Glob, Grep

components.name: README
components.why_use: Reach for this file when you need a single-glance map of every official API surface the repo touches — hooks, sub-agents, agent teams, skills, MCP — so you can navigate to authoritative docs without leaving the project. It is the Core Four 'tools' layer made concrete: knowing what docs exist is prerequisite to wiring hooks or spawning agent teams correctly.

components.name: README
components.why_use: Reach for this when you need to confirm the Vue 3 + TypeScript + Vite stack underpinning the observability dashboard client before wiring hook events into its WebSocket-fed UI — it anchors the frontend substrate so you know which toolchain to extend. In the lesson context it grounds Tactic #7's 'hooks → HTTP → SQLite → WebSocket → Vue dashboard' pipeline to a reproducible scaffold a new contributor can spin up immediately.

components.name: convert_paths_absolute
components.why_use: Reach for this command after cloning or moving a Claude Code project when hook scripts silently break because settings.json still holds relative paths committed from the original machine. In the observability repo context — where every lifecycle hook (send_event.py, pre_tool_use.py, etc.) must resolve correctly before a single event fires — one bad relative path kills the entire hooks pipeline before it starts.

frontmatter.description: Converts relative paths in .claude/settings.json command scripts to absolute paths

components.name: notification.py
components.why_use: Reach for this hook when you're running multi-agent orchestration sessions long enough to context-switch away — TTS ensures you don't miss a permission_prompt or idle_prompt pause that would stall the entire swarm. It embodies Tactic #7's principle that making the invisible visible includes human-attention signals, not just dashboard timelines.

components.name: post_tool_use.py
components.why_use: Reach for this hook whenever you need a zero-friction audit trail of every tool call result across one or more agents — it fires automatically on every PostToolUse event and appends structured payloads to a session-scoped JSON log without ever blocking the agent. In the lesson context this is the persistence layer that makes Tactic #7 real: the observability dashboard has nothing to display until hooks like this one capture and store raw event data from each subagent's context window.

components.name: pre_tool_use.py
components.why_use: Reach for pre_tool_use.py when you need a synchronous enforcement gate that blocks destructive or sensitive tool calls before they execute — critical in multi-agent swarms (Tactic #6) where individual agents run with high autonomy across isolated context windows and no human sitting at each pane. IDD's observability lesson makes explicit that building systems of trust requires both visibility (Tactic #7, the dashboard) and enforcement (this hook); without a blocking guard, the observability pipeline only shows you the damage after it happens.

components.name: send_event.py
components.why_use: Reach for send_event.py whenever you need to wire any Claude Code lifecycle event (PreToolUse, PostToolUse, SubagentStart, Stop, etc.) into an external pipeline — it is the single drop-in forwarder that normalises hook stdin payloads into a timestamped server POST with no per-event boilerplate. As IDD shows in this repo, dropping this script plus twelve thin callers into any project's .claude/hooks/ instantly joins that project to the observability grid, making the invisible multi-agent swarm visible on the Vue dashboard.

components.name: stop.py
components.why_use: Reach for stop.py when you need a reliable session-completion boundary that fires TTS feedback, logs telemetry, and guards against the infinite-hook-loop footgun unique to Stop hooks via the stop_hook_active sentinel. As IDD frames it in the observability lesson, hooks are the mechanism that make the invisible visible — this hook closes the feedback loop by surfacing session-end state to both the dashboard pipeline and the engineer's ears.

components.name: subagent_stop.py
components.why_use: Reach for this hook when you need an audible, zero-configuration signal at every subagent lifecycle boundary — it fires automatically on each SubagentStop event and announces completion via TTS without a human watching the dashboard. As IDD frames it in the observability lesson, making the invisible visible is how engineers build systems of trust with their agents; this hook is the acoustic layer of that observability grid, keeping the operator oriented across a parallel swarm.

components.name: user_prompt_submit.py
components.why_use: Reach for this hook when you need a durable session-scoped record of every user message entering an agent, or when you need a policy gate that can block unsafe prompts before the model ever sees them. In IDD's observability pipeline, UserPromptSubmit is the human-side complement to PreToolUse — together they bracket what the user asked and what the agent did, giving you a complete audit trail for any session.

components.name: constants.py
components.why_use: Reach for this module whenever a hook script needs to resolve or create a session-scoped log path — it centralizes the `CLAUDE_HOOKS_LOG_DIR` env contract so every one of the 12+ hook handlers writes to the same directory tree without duplicating path logic. In the observability pipeline described in the lesson, consistent session directories are what let the Bun server correlate events from parallel subagents back to a single session ID.

components.name: anth.py
components.why_use: Reach for this component when a hook needs to emit natural-language output rather than a static string — for example, generating a personalized completion message after a Stop event. It embodies Core Four model selection in miniature: Haiku is deliberately chosen for fast, cheap in-process inference so the hook adds zero perceptible latency to the agent lifecycle.

components.name: oai.py
components.why_use: Reach for this utility when a hook script needs natural-language LLM output — completion messages, summaries, labels — without embedding raw API boilerplate in every handler; it is the 'model' leg of Core Four abstracted into a single importable helper. It enables the hook observability layer (Tactic #7) to stay expressive and personalized without duplicating client setup across the 12 event scripts.

components.name: summarizer.py
components.why_use: Reach for this when raw hook event payloads need to surface as readable, sub-15-word summaries inside an observability pipeline — the Vue swimlane dashboard IDD demos depends on exactly this kind of just-in-time LLM distillation to label tool calls across a multi-agent swarm. It closes the Core Four loop by turning the model itself into a telemetry layer, making the invisible visible and directly serving the 'systems of trust' mandate from Tactic #7.

components.name: elevenlabs_tts.py
components.why_use: Reach for this when you want hook events to be audible — particularly wired through notification.py so that permission prompts and idle signals speak to you instead of requiring you to watch a dashboard. In IDD's observability pipeline it is the audio channel that complements the visual swimlane view, converting the Tactic #7 event stream into a human-perceptible out-of-band signal during long multi-agent runs.

components.name: openai_tts.py
components.why_use: Reach for this when you want spoken audio feedback as part of your hook observability pipeline — it closes the human-in-the-loop notification cycle with voice alerts instead of silent UI events. In the Tactic #7 context it is the TTS backend behind notification.py: when an agent idles or hits a permission prompt, the engineer hears it rather than hunting a dashboard.

components.name: pyttsx3_tts.py
components.why_use: Reach for this when your hook pipeline needs offline audio feedback to surface agent lifecycle events — permission prompts, idle waits, task completions — to an engineer who isn't watching the terminal. In the lesson's observability stack it is the audio layer that makes the invisible audible without requiring an API key or network call, directly supporting the 'systems of trust' goal IDD describes.

components.name: settings.json
components.why_use: Reach for this component when you need a Claude Code agent to join a multi-agent observability grid instantly — it is the drop-in hook wiring that makes every tool call visible in real time on the dashboard. Per IDD's framing, this settings.json is how you build 'systems of trust' with agents: you cannot debug or improve what you cannot see, and this profile ensures no lifecycle event escapes telemetry.

components.name: README

It also serves as the mental model anchor for Tactic #7: before wiring up hook scripts, read this to understand what each lifecycle event feeds and why the swimlane dashboard exists.

components.name: cc_hook_expert_improve

It encodes the full hook architecture (settings.json topology, all 7 hook events, execution model, JSONL output conventions) so the planner can produce an integration-ready spec without spelunking the codebase first.

components.name: context_bundle_builder.py

components.name: universal_hook_logger.py

It is the canonical starting point for any debugging or audit trail need where you want to reconstruct exactly what events fired and in what order during an agentic run.

components.name: One Word Output

components.name: anth.py
components.why_use: Reach for this component when a hook needs to call an LLM to generate dynamic, human-readable output (e.g. completion messages) rather than emitting static strings. components.name: oai.py
components.why_use: Reach for this module when a Claude Code hook needs fast, cheap LLM-generated natural language output (completion messages, short summaries, dynamic annotations) without spinning up a full agent or incurring Claude API cost. components.name: ollama.py

components.name: openai_tts.py

Use it as the final migration step (5 of N) after all table migrations run, since every index references columns that must already exist.

components.name: 6_functions.sql
components.why_use: Reach for this component when you need database-enforced updated_at consistency across orchestrator tables — it removes the burden from every application-layer write path and guarantees timestamps are always accurate regardless of which client or agent touches a row. Because it uses CREATE OR REPLACE, it is safe to apply in idempotent migration pipelines (CI, re-runs, blue-green deploys) without manual teardown.

components.name: 7_triggers.sql
components.why_use: Reach for this component when you need idempotent database trigger definitions that automatically maintain updated_at timestamps across orchestrator and agent tables — safe to re-run on every migration pass without side effects. components.name: 8_orchestrator_chat.sql
components.why_use: Reach for this component when you need a persistent, append-only log of all multi-directional messages exchanged across a multi-agent orchestration session — it captures user↔orchestrator↔command_agent turns in a single canonical table. The 3-way CHECK constraint and nullable agent_id FK make it the right foundation for any pipeline that needs auditable conversation history without splitting message content across multiple tables.

components.name: README
components.why_use: Reach for this component when onboarding to the orchestration database layer or before authoring a new migration — it maps the full dependency graph (0→7) and explains why idempotent CREATE IF NOT EXISTS is mandatory over destructive DROP TABLE patterns. components.name: adw_ship_iso.py

In the Lesson 8 model this is the 'moving out of the loop' moment: once all prior ADW stages have populated state, this script ships autonomously so the engineer never touches git again.

components.name: adw_test_iso.py
components.why_use: Reach for this component when you need the testing leg of a multi-step ADW pipeline to run autonomously in an isolated worktree — no manual intervention between patch and PR. It embodies Lesson 8's 'moving out of the loop' principle: the engineer fires it once, and agentic test runners, retry logic, and GitHub reporting all execute without you in the conversation.

components.name: __init__.py

components.name: health_check.py

Per Lesson 8, investing engineering time in agentic layer reliability (not one-off manual checks) is exactly how you move out of the loop safely.

components.name: sandbox_poc.py

components.name: test_agents.py
components.why_use: Reach for this component when you need to verify that the ADW agentic infrastructure is correctly wired up before committing engineering time to higher-level workflows — it surfaces model availability and retry-logic failures early, not mid-pipeline. Per Lesson 8, investing in the agentic layer means keeping its primitives provably functional; this smoke test is the health check that earns you confidence to operate out-of-loop.

components.name: test_model_selection.py
components.why_use: Reach for this component when you need to guard your ADW model-routing configuration against silent regressions — it catches the moment a slash command silently gets the wrong intelligence tier (sonnet vs. opus) before it costs you an agentic run. In Lesson 8 terms, this is the validation layer that makes your agentic layer trustworthy enough to run out of the loop without second-guessing every model dispatch.

components.name: test_r2_uploader.py
components.why_use: Reach for this component when you need to verify that your agentic layer's cloud storage infrastructure is correctly provisioned before autonomous agents begin depending on it for artifact persistence. In Lesson 8 terms, you cannot prioritize agentics if the primitives your agents run on are broken — this script is the smoke test that gates R2 into the ring.

components.name: test_webhook_simplified.py
components.why_use: Reach for this script whenever you modify webhook-trigger routing logic and need immediate feedback on which ADW workflows require a pre-existing ADW ID versus which can be cold-started — it surfaces the full workflow contract in a single terminal run without making live HTTP calls. Per Lesson 8's emphasis on building the agentic layer, this validator is part of the feedback infrastructure that keeps your ADW mesh trustworthy as you scale autonomous workflows.

components.name: __init__.py
components.why_use: Reach for this component when you need a declarative entry-point that fires ADW workflows in response to events—keeping the engineer out of the request/response loop entirely. Per Lesson 8, triggers are the thin edge of the agentic ring: they let machines operate with your judgment autonomously so you stop coding one-offs and start solving problem classes.

components.name: adw_trigger_aea_server.py
components.why_use: Reach for this component when you need to embed a persistent, resumable Claude Code agent inside a running web application — it is the production form of Lesson 8's gateway script, wrapping the application layer with a durable server that manages session IDs, subprocess lifecycles, and conversation history so agents can operate without the engineer in the loop. Use it when you are past one-off prompts and actively building the agentic layer ring: machines that ship with your judgment, resuming across client reconnects and server restarts without a human babysitting each step.

components.name: trigger_cron.py
components.why_use: Reach for this component when you want the agentic layer to self-activate on GitHub events rather than waiting for a human to fire the workflow — it embodies Lesson 8's 'Gateway Script' by moving you fully out of the trigger loop. Use it to convert a manually-run ADW into an always-on problem-class solver that ships your judgment autonomously on every qualifying issue.

components.name: trigger_webhook.py
components.why_use: Reach for this component when you need to move fully out of the loop — letting GitHub issue events autonomously fire ADW workflows the moment they land, with no developer in the conversation. It is the gateway script from Lesson 8 made concrete: a thin FastAPI shell that surrounds the agentic layer, absorbs the external signal, and hands off background work so the engineer never has to respond manually.

components.name: README
components.why_use: Reach for this ADW system when you need machines shipping autonomously on GitHub issues without you in the loop — it provides the isolated-worktree infrastructure that lets up to 15 agents run concurrently without filesystem or port collisions. Per Tactic 8, this component IS the agentic layer: the gateway script ring around your codebase that operates with your judgment at scale, moving you firmly out of the conversation loop.

components.name: README

Per Lesson 8, this is the kind of demo that illustrates how a minimal gateway script surrounds application code and lets AI do the heavy lifting, freeing the engineer to operate at the agentic layer.

components.name: create-worktree-subagent
components.why_use: Reach for this component when you need to delegate git worktree creation to a subagent rather than running the slash command inline — it enforces the pattern of using `/create_worktree` instead of raw git commands, ensuring consistent parallel-dev environment setup. It acts as a thin dispatcher that parses branch/port-offset from natural language and hands off to the fully automated slash command.

frontmatter.name: create-worktree-subagent
frontmatter.description: Use when the user explicitly asks for a SUBAGENT to create a worktree. If the user does not mention "subagent" or explicitly request subagent delegation, do NOT trigger this. Only use when user says things like "use a subagent to create a worktree" or "delegate worktree creation to a subagent". Creates isolated git worktrees with parallel-running configuration.
frontmatter.tools: SlashCommand, Bash, Read, Write, Edit, Glob, Grep

components.name: docs-scraper
components.why_use: Reach for this component when you need to pull external documentation offline into a structured markdown corpus — for example, seeding an ai_docs/ reference library before a build sprint or capturing third-party API docs for RAG ingestion. It handles the full fetch-clean-save pipeline autonomously, so engineers don't hand-roll one-off scraping scripts each time new docs land.

frontmatter.name: docs-scraper
frontmatter.description: Documentation scraping specialist. Use proactively to fetch and save documentation from URLs as properly formatted markdown files.

components.name: fetch-docs-haiku45
components.why_use: Reach for this agent when you need a zero-touch documentation scraper that fetches and persists raw docs to disk without summarization or transformation — ideal for benchmarking or seeding a knowledge base. It uses Haiku 4.5 specifically, making it useful when comparing retrieval quality or cost across model tiers.

frontmatter.name: fetch-docs-haiku45
frontmatter.description: Fetch and save documentation from URLs using Haiku 4.5 model. Use for benchmarking documentation retrieval tasks.

components.name: fetch-docs-sonnet45
components.why_use: Reach for this agent when you need a repeatable, model-pinned benchmark for documentation retrieval — it locks the model to Sonnet 4.5 so performance comparisons across model versions stay apples-to-apples. It is also the right pick when you need raw, unmodified doc content scraped and persisted to disk without any summarization or transformation.

frontmatter.name: fetch-docs-sonnet45
frontmatter.description: Fetch and save documentation from URLs using Sonnet 4.5 model. Use for benchmarking documentation retrieval tasks.

components.name: meta-agent
components.why_use: Reach for this component when an engineer needs to scaffold a new Claude Code sub-agent from a plain-English description — it fetches live Anthropic docs before writing so the generated frontmatter stays current with the API. It handles all architectural decisions (name, color, tool selection, system prompt structure) in one shot and writes the file directly, eliminating the boilerplate loop of manually authoring .claude/agents/*.md files.

frontmatter.name: meta-agent
frontmatter.description: Generates a new, complete Claude Code sub-agent configuration file from a user's description. Use this to create new agents. Use this Proactively when the user asks you to create a new sub agent.

components.name: scout-report-suggest-fast
components.why_use: Reach for this component when you need a fast, read-only codebase audit before committing to a fix — it scouts file locations, root causes, and resolution strategies without touching anything. Use it proactively at the start of a debug or refactor cycle to get a structured report of affected files and line numbers before any write agent takes over.

frontmatter.name: scout-report-suggest-fast
frontmatter.description: Use proactively to quickly scout codebase issues, identify problem locations, and suggest resolutions. Specialist for read-only analysis and reporting without making changes.

components.name: scout-report-suggest
components.why_use: Reach for this agent when you need a safe, non-destructive reconnaissance pass before committing to a fix — it produces a structured, line-precise SCOUT REPORT that a write-enabled coder agent can act on without re-reading the codebase. It is the canonical first step when the problem location is unknown or the blast radius of a blind edit is too high.

frontmatter.name: scout-report-suggest
frontmatter.description: Use proactively to scout codebase issues, identify problem locations, and suggest resolutions. Specialist for read-only analysis and reporting without making changes.

components.name: find_and_summarize
components.why_use: Reach for this command when you need a reproducible, structured inventory of all files in a directory before planning a refactor, agent handoff, or RAG-index build — it enforces an incremental read discipline (50→100→200 lines per file) that prevents hallucinated summaries from partial context. The YAML output makes downstream automation straightforward: feed it to a planner, diff it across branches, or embed it as agent context without further parsing.

frontmatter.description: Finds and summarizes specific files in the codebase and saves the summary to app_docs directory

components.name: load_ai_docs
components.why_use: Reach for this component when you need to benchmark multi-agent documentation retrieval pipelines — it orchestrates model-specific subagents to fetch URLs, persist markdown, and answer structured Q&A, making it ideal for evaluating agent capability across retrieval + file I/O + QA dimensions. It enforces a strict delegation pattern (subagent does all fetching/saving, orchestrator only coordinates) that stress-tests Task-tool dispatch and subagent naming priority systems.

frontmatter.description: Fetch and save AI documentation using model-specific subagents for benchmarking

components.name: plan_new_feature
components.why_use: Reach for this command when a feature request needs to be crystallized into a reviewable spec before any code is written — it enforces the stop-coding discipline by saving the plan as a durable markdown artifact in specs/ so a human or downstream agent can review and approve it before implementation begins. It operationalizes the explore-plan-code tactic by making the planning step a first-class, named deliverable rather than ephemeral chain-of-thought, and explicitly prohibits subagents and code generation to keep the model focused on reasoning over building.

frontmatter.description: Creates a concise engineering implementation plan based on user requirements and saves it to specs directory

components.name: build
components.why_use: Reach for this command when you have a completed plan document and want a single slash-command to drive the full implementation loop: it reads the plan, ultrathinks through it, executes the changes, and surfaces a diff-stat summary. It enforces the plan-first discipline by halting immediately if no plan path is supplied, keeping the engineer honest about planning before coding.

frontmatter.description: Build the codebase based on the plan

components.name: convert_paths_absolute
components.why_use: Reach for this command when relative paths in .claude/settings.json command scripts break under execution from unexpected working directories. It is a one-shot environment normalization tool that makes the agent's tool configuration portable and location-independent.

frontmatter.description: Converts relative paths in .claude/settings.json command scripts to absolute paths

components.name: create_worktree_prompt
components.why_use: Reach for this component when you need to spin up a fully-isolated parallel development environment — separate ports, separate SQLite DB, and separate hook configuration — without touching the main repo. It automates the entire worktree lifecycle (create, configure, start) in a single invocation, eliminating the manual coordination overhead that causes port collisions and hook misconfiguration across concurrent Claude instances.

components.name: list_worktrees_prompt
components.why_use: Reach for this component when you need a live snapshot of all parallel worktree environments — port assignments, service health, and env config — without manually grepping each branch. It surfaces active vs. stopped services across the trees/ layout so an engineer can orient quickly before launching or debugging a multi-worktree workflow.

frontmatter.description: List all git worktrees with their configuration and status

components.name: load_ai_docs
components.why_use: Reach for this command when agent workflows need up-to-date third-party library docs vendored locally as markdown context files — it scrapes, caches with a 24-hour TTL, and fans out fetches in parallel so you never block on stale or missing docs. It is the canonical setup step before any coding session that relies on AI-adjacent libraries whose docs change frequently.

frontmatter.description: Load documentation from their respective websites into local markdown files our agents can use as context.

components.name: prime

It enforces the 'understand before you act' discipline by making codebase orientation a single invocable primitive rather than a manual multi-step ritual.

components.name: quick-plan

It is the canonical 'stop and plan' gate in a TAC workflow, producing a durable artifact in specs/ that can be handed directly to a coding agent or human developer.

components.name: start
components.why_use: Reach for this component when you need a one-keystroke way to boot the full local dev stack inside a Claude Code session without leaving the editor context. It delegates to a shell script so the startup sequence stays maintainable in one place while the command itself stays trivially simple.

components.name: t_metaprompt_workflow

It parallelizes documentation fetching via Task+WebFetch and enforces a strict output schema, making it the right tool when standing up new workflow commands without manual prompt engineering.

frontmatter.description: Create a new prompt

components.name: hitl_example.py
components.why_use: Reach for this component when you need to pause agent execution and surface a decision point to a human operator — whether that's approving a destructive action, answering a free-form question, or selecting from multiple options. It demonstrates the canonical HITL integration pattern using ask_question/ask_permission/ask_choice utilities that route through the observability server and client dashboard.

components.name: notification.py
components.why_use: Reach for this component when you want Claude Code to audibly interrupt the engineer the moment the agent pauses for input — it auto-selects the best available TTS backend (ElevenLabs → OpenAI → pyttsx3) so you get voice alerts without wiring any TTS plumbing yourself. It fires on the Notification hook event, making it a zero-config drop-in for any repo where the developer works heads-down and needs an out-of-band signal when the agent stalls.

components.name: post_tool_use.py
components.why_use: Reach for this component when you need passive, zero-configuration capture of every tool invocation's output within a Claude Code session — it silently appends each PostToolUse payload to a per-session JSONL-style log without any agent awareness. It is the canonical starting point for session replay, audit trails, or downstream analytics that need a complete tool-call history without modifying agent behavior.

components.name: pre_compact.py
components.why_use: Reach for this hook when you need passive observability into Claude Code's context-compaction lifecycle — it fires automatically before every compaction, capturing the full input payload to a JSON log and optionally snapshotting the raw transcript so you can audit what context was discarded. It is also your safety net for recovery: if a compaction silently drops critical session state, the transcript backup gives you a restore point without any manual intervention.

components.name: pre_tool_use.py
components.why_use: Reach for this component when you need an autonomous last-line-of-defence against destructive filesystem operations inside agentic Claude Code sessions — it intercepts every Bash tool call before execution and blocks rm -rf patterns unless the target path is explicitly allowlisted. It is the canonical example of a PreToolUse safety guard: zero configuration at call-time, surgical path parsing, and a clear allowlist escape hatch for legitimate tree-pruning directories.

components.name: send_event.py
components.why_use: Reach for this hook when you need real-time, centralized visibility into Claude Code lifecycle events across one or more agent sessions — it bridges the local hook stdin/stdout contract to an HTTP observability server, optionally enriching each event with an AI-generated summary and the active model name extracted from the session transcript. It is the canonical pattern for multi-agent telemetry collection where a single server must aggregate PreToolUse/PostToolUse signals from many concurrent Claude Code processes without any manual intervention.

components.name: session_end.py
components.why_use: Reach for this component when you need passive session-boundary observability — it fires automatically at Claude Code session end to capture timing, message count, and exit reason without any human or agent intervention. It is a zero-touch audit trail builder: once wired into hooks config it silently accumulates session statistics and raw event logs to local JSON files, giving you a durable record for debugging, billing estimation, or agent-loop analytics.

components.name: session_start.py
components.why_use: Reach for this component when you need zero-touch session observability — it fires automatically on every Claude Code SessionStart, captures git branch and dirty-file count, and appends a structured JSON record to logs/session_start.json without any manual instrumentation. It is the canonical pattern for building an audit trail of when agents begin work, pairing naturally with PostToolUse or Stop hooks that close the loop.

components.name: stop.py
components.why_use: Reach for this component when you want automatic sensory feedback (audio + LLM-generated summary) at the end of every agentic session without manual intervention — it fires on Claude's Stop event and requires zero operator action. It also doubles as a session telemetry sink, writing JSONL receipts to local disk, so it serves both human-notification and audit-trail roles in a single hook.

components.name: subagent_stop.py
components.why_use: Reach for this hook when running long multi-agent workflows where you need ambient awareness that a subagent has finished without watching the terminal — it fires automatically on every Stop event and dispatches an audio TTS announcement via a priority-ranked provider chain (ElevenLabs → OpenAI → pyttsx3). It is the agentic equivalent of a build-complete chime: zero-touch feedback that lets you context-switch away and still notice completion.

components.name: test_hitl.py
components.why_use: Reach for this component when you need to validate that a HITL (Human-in-the-Loop) permission gate works end-to-end before wiring it into a real agent hook — it simulates a dangerous command approval request against a live dashboard. It is a developer smoke-test harness, not a production hook, so use it during local development to confirm the ask_permission flow resolves correctly before trusting it with actual destructive operations.

components.name: user_prompt_submit.py
components.why_use: Reach for this hook when you need zero-overhead, per-message audit trails and session state without touching the agent's core logic — it fires automatically on every UserPromptSubmit, appending raw prompt payloads to a flat JSON log and building a per-session prompt history file in .claude/data/sessions/. It also supports lazy LLM-powered agent-name annotation, making it a foundation for session replay, cost attribution, and human-review pipelines.

components.name: constants.py
components.why_use: Reach for this component when you need a single source of truth for session-scoped log path resolution across multiple hooks — it centralizes the LOG_BASE_DIR env override and the mkdir logic so individual hooks never duplicate path-construction code. It acts as a shared utility layer that keeps hook scripts thin and consistent, which matters when hooks fan out across PreToolUse, PostToolUse, and Stop events.

components.name: hitl.py
components.why_use: Reach for this component when a hook needs to pause agentic execution mid-flight and gate a tool call behind explicit human approval, a yes/no question, or a constrained choice — it spins up an ephemeral local WebSocket server so the observability dashboard can push the human's answer back into the hook's thread. It is the canonical pattern for keeping a human in the decision loop without blocking the Claude process on stdin or polling.

components.name: anth.py
components.why_use: Reach for this when you need a fast, low-overhead Anthropic call inside a Claude Code hook — it handles env loading, client instantiation, and error suppression in one import. The `generate_completion_message()` function is the canonical pattern for adding dynamic, personalized LLM-generated feedback to Stop or PostToolUse hooks without blocking the agent loop.

components.name: oai.py
components.why_use: Reach for this component when a hook needs to call an LLM mid-task to generate natural language output (e.g., dynamic completion messages) without blocking the main pipeline — it wraps OpenAI's fastest model behind a safe, exception-swallowing interface. It is the base utility layer for any hook that needs LLM enrichment rather than deterministic string formatting.

components.name: model_extractor.py
components.why_use: Reach for this when a hook needs to know which Claude model is active in the current session without hard-coding model names — it parses the JSONL transcript to extract the model from the most recent assistant message and optionally caches the result so repeated hook invocations don't re-scan the file on every event. Note: ENABLE_CACHING is currently False, so the file-based cache path is dead code in practice; the component always does a live transcript read.

components.name: summarizer.py
components.why_use: Reach for this when you need a human-readable one-liner overlaid on raw hook-event JSON in a monitoring TUI, audit log, or Telegram notification — it converts opaque payloads into engineer-digestible present-tense summaries without bespoke per-event display logic. It is a zero-config drop-in because it delegates all NLU to an LLM call, so it handles novel event types gracefully without requiring schema updates.

components.name: elevenlabs_tts.py
components.why_use: Reach for this component when you need real-time audio feedback wired into a Claude Code hook — e.g., a PostToolUse or Stop hook that reads completion status or error messages aloud via ElevenLabs Flash v2.5 (~75ms latency). It is a thin CLI-invocable TTS utility living under .claude/hooks/utils/, designed to be shelled out from a parent hook script rather than run as a hook directly; uncertainty flag: the file has no hook event wiring itself, so it acts as a called utility, not an autonomous hook listener.

components.name: openai_tts.py
components.why_use: Reach for this component when a hook event (Stop, PostToolUse, etc.) needs to surface agent activity as spoken audio rather than terminal text — it turns any string into streamed, played-back speech with a single subprocess call. It is the canonical TTS leaf in the hooks/utils layer, meaning you wire it from a hook script rather than building your own OpenAI audio pipeline.

components.name: pyttsx3_tts.py
components.why_use: Reach for this component when you want an agent hook to provide offline, zero-API-key audio feedback at task completion — no cloud dependency, no credential management. It is a drop-in PostToolUse or Stop hook that speaks a random or caller-supplied message via the system TTS engine, giving the engineer a heads-up without watching a terminal.

components.name: Bullet Points
components.why_use: Reach for this component when you need an agent or LLM to produce structured, scannable output — particularly for task breakdowns, step-by-step runbooks, or multi-level analysis where hierarchy communicates relationships. It enforces strict nesting discipline and action-item tagging, making it ideal for agentic workflows where downstream consumers (human or machine) need to parse output reliably.

frontmatter.name: Bullet Points
frontmatter.description: Hierarchical bullet points for quick scanning

components.name: GenUI

It is an output-style hook that automatically materialises every response as a fully self-contained, browser-ready HTML document, eliminating the manual copy-paste-to-browser step from the agentic workflow.

frontmatter.name: GenUI

components.name: HTML Structured

It enforces semantic HTML5 conventions (article/section/aside) and data-attribute contracts that make agent output machine-consumable as well as readable.

frontmatter.name: HTML Structured

components.name: Markdown Focused

It enforces information architecture discipline (hierarchy, whitespace, visual grouping) that makes agent-generated docs and analysis reports significantly easier to parse than plain prose.

frontmatter.name: Markdown Focused

components.name: observable-tools-diffs-tts

It is especially useful on long agentic runs where the developer is away from the screen and wants an audio ping when work completes, combined with a structured audit trail of exactly what changed and how.

components.name: observable-tools-diffs
components.why_use: Reach for this output style when you want every Claude Code session to self-document its own actions — it forces the agent to emit a chronological tool-call log and git diff after each response, making agentic work fully auditable without external tooling. It is especially valuable in pair-programming or review workflows where a human needs to verify exactly what the agent touched and in what order.

components.name: Table Based
components.why_use: Reach for this component when you want Claude to present structured data, comparisons, or multi-step processes in a scannable tabular format rather than prose or bullet lists. It reduces cognitive load during code reviews, config audits, and analysis outputs by forcing information into rows and columns that can be parsed at a glance.

frontmatter.name: Table Based

components.name: TTS Summary
components.why_use: Reach for this component when you want Claude Code to deliver a spoken end-of-turn summary via ElevenLabs TTS, giving the operator an audio confirmation of what was accomplished without needing to read the terminal. It pairs well with long-running agentic sessions where the engineer steps away and wants a verbal 'done' signal rather than polling the screen.

frontmatter.name: TTS Summary

components.name: TTS Summary
